2.ctx: Jesus is back in Capernaum, probably at Peter’s house (1:29). This is the first of five conflict stories (2:1–3:6) in which religious leaders object to what Jesus says and does, ending with a plot to kill him (3:6). Houses had flat roofs reached by an outside stair. The Old Testament teaches that forgiving sins belongs to God (Exodus 34:7; Isaiah 43:25).
2.mean: The house is so packed that nobody else can get near the door. Jesus is speaking God’s word to them, the good news of God’s kingdom. Four men arrive carrying a paralysed friend on a mat. They cannot get in, so they climb onto the roof, dig through it and lower him down right in front of Jesus. Jesus sees ‘their faith’, the faith that would not give up, and then says something nobody expects: ‘Son, your sins are forgiven.’ They came for healing; Jesus starts with forgiveness. He goes to the deepest need first. Some scribes sitting there are shocked. ‘He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?’ They are right about one thing: only God can forgive sins against him. If Jesus is only a man, he has claimed what belongs to God. Jesus knows what they are thinking and asks a sharp question: which is easier, to tell a paralysed man his sins are forgiven, or to tell him to get up and walk? Saying ‘your sins are forgiven’ is easy, because nobody can see whether it has happened. Saying ‘get up and walk’ is tested on the spot. So Jesus does the visible thing to prove the invisible: ‘so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins…’ He tells the man to get up, pick up his mat and go home. The man stands, picks up his mat and walks out in front of everyone. The crowd are astounded and praise God; they have never seen anything like it. Mark wants you to face the scribes’ question. Either Jesus is a blasphemer, or he has the authority of God himself. The healing settles which it is. And the forgiveness the man received is offered to everyone who comes to Jesus, whether or not they are carried there by friends.
2.big: Jesus forgives a paralysed man’s sins and then heals him, proving that he, the Son of Man, has God’s authority on earth to forgive.

vv.h: they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat
b: Wesley explains that flat roofs had a covering or trap door, which the friends took up and then ‘broke the passage wider’ to let the mat through. Cooper pictures the falling debris and the shock to the house owner. Mark tells it simply; the effort itself shows how much they believed Jesus could help. The ESV Study Bible describes such a roof as branches or sticks combined with clay; Luke adds that this one had tiles (Luke 5:19).

vv.h: When Jesus saw their faith
b: Whose faith? The four friends’ certainly. Calvin thought ‘their’ also included the paralysed man, because ‘the paralytic could not have obtained the forgiveness of his sins, if he had had no faith of his own.’ English thinks it more likely that the sick man shared it too. Calvin added that faith was visible in their ‘laboriousness’: they would not have taken such trouble without confidence in Jesus. The faith of friends can bring someone to Jesus; each person must still receive his forgiveness for themselves.

vv.h: Son, your sins are forgiven
b: ‘Son’ is a word of affection. Was the man’s illness caused by sin? Jesus does not say so, and elsewhere he denies that suffering is always punishment for a person’s own sin (John 9:2–3). Calvin thought Jesus went to the root of all human trouble, our separation from God, before dealing with the symptom. Cooper notes that in Mark this is the only place where Jesus explicitly forgives someone’s sins.

vv.h: He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?
b: Blasphemy is speaking against God or claiming what belongs to him. Calvin thought the scribes were too quick to take the worst meaning, since prophets also announced God’s forgiveness. Wesley saw the first opposition coming from the learned, not from ordinary people: ‘See whence the first offense cometh!’ The same charge of blasphemy will be Jesus’ death sentence (14:64).

vv.h: Which is easier
b: English explains: it is easier to say ‘your sins are forgiven’, because no one can check it; to say ‘get up and walk’ is to face an immediate test. Cooper puts it the other way round: saying either is easy, but doing either is impossible without God’s power. Both readings reach the same point: the healing is visible proof of the forgiveness.

vv.h: the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins
b: This is the first time Jesus calls himself ‘the Son of Man’ in Mark; he will use the title often. The phrase can mean simply a human being, as in Psalm 8:4, but English thinks it more likely draws on Daniel’s vision of ‘One like the Son of Man’ who is given ‘dominion, glory, and kingship’ (Daniel 7:13–14). The one who will judge at the end can forgive now, ‘on earth’.

vv.h: We have never seen anything like this!
b: Isaiah had promised that in the age of salvation ‘the lame will leap like a deer’ (Isaiah 35:6). The people glorify God, as they should, though they do not yet grasp who Jesus is. English notes that even here there is no compelling proof: people still had to take Jesus’ word for the forgiveness. Faith is invited, not forced.

The Psalms join forgiveness and healing: God is the one ‘who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases’ (Psalm 103:3). Jesus does both, and in that order. God says, ‘I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions’ (Isaiah 43:25); Jesus does what God does.
After his resurrection Jesus gives his followers a share in declaring forgiveness in his name (John 20:23); the authority behind it remains his (1 John 1:9).

l.t: He forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.
God blots out transgressions for his own sake.
One like the Son of Man given dominion.
The lame will leap like a deer.
Matthew: the crowd praised God for giving such authority to men.
Luke: Pharisees and teachers had come from every village.
Suffering is not always punishment for one’s own sin.
The charge of blasphemy at Jesus’ trial.

qs: What did the four friends do to get the paralysed man to Jesus, and what did Jesus say first?
Why were the scribes right that only God can forgive sins, and what does that mean for who Jesus is?
Who might you ‘carry’ to Jesus through prayer, friendship or practical help?

2.ctx: Mark places the booth ‘beside the sea’, probably at or near Capernaum, which lay on the road to Damascus and had a tax post. Tax collectors in Galilee worked under Herod Antipas’s system and were often seen as extortioners (English). Matthew’s Gospel tells the same story about ‘Matthew’ (Matthew 9:9), and lists Matthew the tax collector among the Twelve (Matthew 10:3).
2.mean: Jesus is teaching by the lake again, and as he walks along he sees Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at his tax booth. ‘Follow Me,’ Jesus says, and Levi gets up and follows him. Mark tells it in one breath, just as he told the call of the fishermen. But this call is more shocking. Fishermen were respectable working men. Tax collectors were seen as traitors who grew rich at their neighbours’ expense. Calvin saw Levi’s call as an example of ‘Christ’s undeserved goodness’: Jesus calls people not because they are good, but because he is gracious. Then comes a dinner at Levi’s house. ‘Many tax collectors and sinners’ are there, eating with Jesus and his disciples. ‘Sinners’ here means people known for not keeping God’s law, or for not keeping the Pharisees’ strict rules about it. Eating together meant friendship and acceptance, so the scribes who were Pharisees are offended. They ask the disciples, ‘Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?’ Jesus answers with a proverb and a statement of his mission. ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.’ A doctor who avoided sick people would be useless. ‘I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.’ Jesus is not saying the Pharisees had no need of him. He is saying that only those who know they are sick will come to the doctor. The people who thought they were fine kept their distance; the people who knew they were not came to the table. Jesus’ welcome does not mean he approves of everything they did; Levi left his booth behind. But the welcome comes first. Mark wants you to see that no one is too far gone for Jesus to call, and that the only thing that keeps anyone from his table is thinking they do not need it.
2.big: Jesus calls a despised tax collector to follow him and eats with sinners, because he came, like a doctor, for those who know they are sick.

vv.h: Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth
b: Levi is identified with the Matthew of Matthew 9:9, the traditional identification, which English accepts. English notes a small puzzle: Mark also calls James ‘son of Alphaeus’ (3:18), and he does not explain whether Levi and James were brothers. English explains that tax collectors in Galilee worked for Herod Antipas’s system and mostly extorted more than was required. The ESV Study Bible suggests that a tax booth ‘beside the sea’ (2:13) was used for taxing fishermen.

vv.h: Follow Me
b: The same call as to the fishermen (1:17), and the same immediate response. Cooper notes that Levi left behind a very profitable business. English sees in Levi someone used to making hard decisions and living with them.

vv.h: many tax collectors and sinners were eating with Him and His disciples
b: Wesley thought some were ‘doubtless invited by Matthew’ out of concern for his old friends, while many simply pressed in uninvited because they wanted to hear Jesus. The BSB reads ‘Levi’s house’; English notes that the original says only ‘his house’, which could also mean the house where Jesus was staying. At a formal meal guests reclined on couches, and the ESV Study Bible notes that reclining together showed personal acceptance and friendship.

vv.h: the scribes who were Pharisees
b: The Pharisees were a movement devoted to careful keeping of the Law, including rules about food and purity. Cooper notes that to them ‘sinners’ included anyone who did not follow their interpretation of Scripture. Eating with such people risked uncleanness.

vv.h: It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick
b: Wesley read it as gentle irony: ‘if these were righteous I should not call them. But now, they are the very persons I came to save.’ Calvin said the scribes erred in two ways: they forgot what Christ had come to do, and they excused their own faults while despising others. Matthew adds Jesus’ words from Hosea, ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice’ (Matthew 9:13; Hosea 6:6).

Jesus’ meals with outsiders run through the Gospels: he is called ‘a friend of tax collectors and sinners’ (Luke 7:34). Luke tells of another tax collector, Zacchaeus, and Jesus’ words: ‘the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost’ (Luke 19:10).

Paul calls himself the worst of sinners and says Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). The doctor image runs back to God’s words to Israel: ‘I am the LORD who heals you’ (Exodus 15:26).

l.t: Matthew: ‘I desire mercy, not sacrifice.’
Luke: Levi held a great banquet; ‘sinners to repentance’.
I desire mercy, not sacrifice.
Tax collectors and sinners draw near; the lost sheep.
Zacchaeus: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.
Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.
Levi’s fellow disciples: the Twelve.

qs: Who comes to Levi’s dinner, and who objects?
What does Jesus mean by comparing himself to a doctor? Who are ‘the healthy’?
Are there people you find it hard to imagine Jesus calling? What does Levi’s story say to you about them, and about yourself?

b: Capernaum stood on the road linking the region with Damascus, and the Lexham Bible Dictionary describes it as a centre of commerce and a Roman tax station; a Roman milestone has been found near its synagogue. If Levi’s booth was in Capernaum (Mark does not name the town), it fits what is known of it. See the history note on Capernaum at Mark 1:21.

2.ctx: The Law commanded a fast only on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29). Pious Pharisees fasted much more often, twice a week (Luke 18:12), which English and Cooper say was Mondays and Thursdays. John the Baptist’s disciples also fasted; English suggests their teacher’s imprisonment (1:14) may have given them a particular reason.
2.mean: Fasting means going without food for a time, usually to pray, to mourn or to show sorrow for sin. John’s disciples and the Pharisees fasted often. Jesus’ disciples did not, and people noticed: ‘Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?’ Jesus answers with a picture everyone knew: a wedding. Cooper notes that a wedding was a time of feasting and great joy. Nobody fasts at a wedding while the bridegroom is there. ‘How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?’ Jesus speaks of himself as the bridegroom (Calvin: he ‘compares himself to the bridegroom’), and his coming is a time of joy, not mourning. In the Old Testament, God himself is pictured as the bridegroom or husband of his people: ‘as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you’ (Isaiah 62:5). English suggests Jesus may be hinting at that role, though only the eye of faith would see it then. Then the mood changes: ‘But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.’ Cooper calls this the first indication in Mark that Jesus was fully aware of his mission, and English sees a hint of Jesus’ death. The joy of his presence will be followed by sorrow, and the disciples will fast then. So Jesus is not against fasting. He is against fasting as a fixed rule that ignores what God is doing. Fasting fits times of waiting, longing and sorrow; it does not fit the moment when the long-awaited bridegroom has arrived. Calvin drew out a lesson for Christians: do not make outward practices a test of holiness, and do not try to make everyone follow your own pattern of devotion. The early church did fast (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23), in the time between Jesus’ going away and his coming again. Christians still live in that time: the bridegroom has been ‘taken’, and they long for his return, yet he is with them by his Spirit.
2.big: Jesus’ disciples do not fast because the bridegroom has come, a time for joy, but he warns that he will be taken away and then they will fast.

vv.h: Why don’t Your disciples fast
b: Calvin thought the Pharisees were trying to stir up rivalry between John’s disciples and Jesus’ disciples, and warned against breaking the unity of faith over outward ceremonies. Cooper notes that some Pharisees made sure others saw them fasting (compare Matthew 6:16–18).

vv.h: How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?
b: The BSB’s ‘guests’ translates a Hebrew-style phrase, which Calvin explains as a Hebrew phrase, ‘the children of the bridegroom, or of the nuptial bed’, meaning the wedding guests. Calvin says Christ ‘compares himself to the bridegroom’. John the Baptist had called Jesus the bridegroom and himself the bridegroom’s friend (John 3:29). The Old Testament pictures God as Israel’s husband (Isaiah 54:5; Hosea 2:19).

vv.h: the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them
b: Cooper calls this the first indication in Mark that Jesus knew where his mission would lead; English agrees that it hints at Jesus’ death. Calvin noted that Jesus was easing his disciples into hardship gradually, sparing them while he was with them. The ESV Study Bible hears an echo of the Servant who ‘was taken away’ (Isaiah 53:8).
The prophets looked forward to the day when fasts would become feasts (Zechariah 8:19). Jesus’ coming begins that joy, though the full wedding feast lies ahead (Revelation 19:7–9).

Jesus assumes his followers will fast (Matthew 6:16–18), and the early church fasted when seeking God’s guidance (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23). Christians differ in how they practise it, for example in set seasons such as Lent or in personal times of prayer, but in Scripture fasting goes with prayer and seeking God (Acts 13:2–3).

l.t: As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you.
I will betroth you to Me forever.
The fasts will become joyful feasts.
Matthew: ‘Can the guests of the bridegroom mourn?’
Luke’s account of the same question.
John the Baptist: the friend of the bridegroom.
The wedding supper of the Lamb.
The church at Antioch fasts and prays.

qs: Why, according to Jesus, do his disciples not fast while he is with them?
What does Jesus mean by calling himself the bridegroom, and what does ‘taken from them’ point to?
Is there a spiritual practice you treat as a rule for its own sake? How might it help you seek God instead?

2.ctx: Jesus continues his answer about fasting with two everyday pictures. Wine was stored in skins, and new wine, still fermenting, needed flexible skins that could expand (Cooper). Luke adds a third saying about old wine (Luke 5:39).
2.mean: Jesus finishes his answer with two pictures from ordinary life. First, the patch. If you sew a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old coat, the first time it gets wet the new patch shrinks, pulls away and makes the tear worse. Second, the wineskins. New wine is still fermenting. Pour it into old, dried-out, brittle skins and the gas will burst them, and you lose both the wine and the skins. ‘Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.’ What is Jesus saying? Something new has arrived with him, and it cannot simply be added onto old ways of doing things. On the most common reading among the commentators used here (English, Cooper), the joy of the bridegroom’s presence does not fit the old pattern of regular fasting, just as new wine does not fit old skins, and more broadly the life of God’s kingdom needs a new shape. The forgiveness he offers (2:5), his welcome to sinners (2:17) and his authority over the Sabbath (2:28) all burst the old expectations. Notice what Jesus does not say. He does not say the old was bad. Old coats and old skins were good things. Jesus came to fulfil the Law and the Prophets, not to abolish them (Matthew 5:17), and English stresses that he is not saying the old should be discarded. But the new life he brings must be allowed to take its own shape. Christians have applied these pictures in different ways, and there is a real question about what exactly the old and new stand for (see Where readings differ). Calvin, for example, thought Jesus was talking about not loading new disciples with burdens they were not ready to bear. Either way, the sayings warn against forcing the life of God’s kingdom into old moulds, whether the strict rules of the Pharisees or our own habits and traditions.
2.big: With pictures of a patch and wineskins, Jesus teaches that the new life of God’s kingdom cannot be squeezed into old patterns; it needs new forms.

vv.h: No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment
b: Cooper explains the picture: the unshrunk patch shrinks when washed and tears the old cloth. English: the old cannot simply absorb the new as an add-on; the new surpasses what went before, and the old should not force it into its own shape.

vv.h: new wine is poured into new wineskins
b: New wine needs flexible skins that can stretch as it ferments (Cooper). Wesley’s version notes that ‘bottles’ means ‘sacks of skin’. Luke adds that people who have drunk old wine prefer it (Luke 5:39); Calvin took this as a warning to the Pharisees not to give a received custom undue weight.

2.diff: What are the old and the new? English and Cooper take the old garment and old wineskins to be the existing pattern of religious practice (English: the structure of Jewish ceremonial), and the new cloth and new wine to be the life of the kingdom Jesus brings, which needs new forms. Cooper goes further, saying Jesus came not to reform Judaism but to bring something new, the church; English, by contrast, stresses that Jesus is not saying the old should be discarded, and Jesus himself said he came not to abolish the Law and the Prophets (Matthew 5:17). Calvin rejected the view that the old garments stand for the Pharisees, saying it has ‘no probability on their side’. He read the sayings as being about Jesus’ disciples: they were new and weak, and must not be crushed by a stricter discipline than they could bear, so ‘we ought to spare the weak’. Both readings fit the setting of the fasting question.

b: The prophets promised something new from God: ‘Behold, I am about to do something new’ (Isaiah 43:19), and a new covenant written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Jesus later speaks of ‘the new covenant in My blood’ at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20).

Paul wrestles with the same question in Galatians: whether the new life in Christ must be lived within the old forms of the Law. His answer is that ‘neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation’ (Galatians 6:15).

l.t: Matthew: both the new wine and the new wineskins are preserved.
Luke adds: ‘The old is better.’
Behold, I am about to do something new.
A new covenant written on the heart.
If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.
What counts is a new creation.

qs: What happens when new cloth is sewn on an old garment, or new wine is put in old skins?
What ‘new thing’ in 2:1–20 does not fit the old patterns?
Are there habits or traditions in your life that make it hard for God to do something new?

2.ctx: God commanded Israel to rest on the seventh day, even at harvest time (Exodus 20:8–11; 34:21). The Law allowed a hungry traveller to pick grain by hand from a neighbour’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25); the issue here is doing it on the Sabbath. Later Jewish teaching, collected in the Mishnah (Shabbat 7:2), lists thirty-nine main kinds of forbidden work, with reaping among the first.
2.mean: On a Sabbath, Jesus and his disciples walk through a field, and the disciples pick heads of grain as they go. The Pharisees object that they are breaking the Sabbath. Picking grain was allowed on other days (Deuteronomy 23:25), but in the Pharisees’ view it counted as reaping, which was work, and work was forbidden on the Sabbath. Jesus answers from Scripture, reminding them what David did when he and his men were hungry. When David was fleeing from King Saul, the priest gave him the holy bread from the tabernacle, which by law only the priests could eat (1 Samuel 21:1–6; Leviticus 24:5–9). Human need came before the ritual rule, and Scripture does not condemn David. If David could do that, Jesus’ disciples are not guilty for picking grain when hungry. Then Jesus states a principle that only Mark records: ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.’ God gave the Sabbath as a gift: a day of rest, freedom and worship. It was meant to serve people, not to burden them with rules that defeat its purpose. Calvin noted that Jesus is not abolishing the Sabbath here, but showing ‘what is the proper use of it’. Finally comes the boldest claim: ‘Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.’ The Sabbath was God’s own day (Exodus 20:10). To be its Lord is to stand where God stands. As Wesley put it, the supreme Lawgiver has power over his own laws. Mark’s story is building: Jesus forgives sins, welcomes sinners, replaces fasting with feasting, and now claims authority over the Sabbath itself. In the next scene the Pharisees begin plotting to kill him (3:6). For Christians today the passage raises the question of how the Sabbath command applies now, and Christian traditions answer it differently (see the note on Matthew 12:1–8).
2.big: Defending his hungry disciples, Jesus teaches that the Sabbath was given for human good and claims that he, the Son of Man, is Lord even of the Sabbath.

vv.h: His disciples began to pick the heads of grain
b: The Mishnah, a later collection of Jewish legal rulings, lists sowing, ploughing, reaping, threshing, winnowing and grinding among the thirty-nine kinds of work forbidden on the Sabbath (Shabbat 7:2). Luke adds that the disciples rubbed the grain in their hands (Luke 6:1), which Cooper notes the Pharisees could count as threshing too.

vv.h: Have you never read what David did
b: Calvin: ‘If David’s necessity excused him, the same argument ought to be admitted in the case of others.’ He adds that Jesus takes for granted that David was blameless. English notes that Jesus does not defend breaking the Sabbath as such; he points to a principle that matters more, human need.

vv.h: During the high priesthood of Abiathar
b: In 1 Samuel 21 the priest who gave David the bread is Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar escaped Saul’s massacre of the priests soon after and became high priest under David (1 Samuel 22:20). How Mark’s wording fits 1 Samuel is discussed in Where readings differ.

vv.h: The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath
b: Calvin notes that this saying is ‘related by Mark alone’, and that ‘they are mistaken, I think, who suppose that in this passage the Sabbath is entirely abolished; for Christ simply informs us what is the proper use of it.’ Wesley: the Sabbath was made for man ‘And therefore must give way to man’s necessity.’ English observes that the general point can also be found in rabbinic teaching; the new thing is who says it, and what he says next.

vv.h: Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath
b: Wesley: ‘Being the supreme Lawgiver, he hath power to dispense with his own laws’. English notes that ‘Son of Man’ can sometimes mean simply ‘a person’, but he and the other commentators read it here as Jesus speaking of himself, as in 2:10. Cooper sees here Jesus’ claim to lordship over the Law.

2.diff: Abiathar or Ahimelech (2:26)? In 1 Samuel 21 the priest is Ahimelech, but Mark’s Greek names Abiathar, his son. Readings: (1) ‘In the passage about Abiathar’. A. R. Millard (New Bible Dictionary) argues that the phrase is better rendered this way, as in Mark 12:26, where ‘about the burning bush’ refers to a section of Scripture. (2) ‘In the days of Abiathar’. Wesley read it as ‘In the time of Abiathar, who was afterward the high priest’: the events happened in Abiathar’s day, and he is named by the title he later held; the New Bible Dictionary notes that he was high priest during David’s reign. The ESV Study Bible gives both of these first two readings as possible. (3) A slip. English lists suggestions (a copyist’s addition, an early Jewish-style exposition of the story, or someone working from memory) and concludes, ‘It is a mistake’; he notes that some manuscripts leave out the phrase, as Matthew and Luke do. He argues that Mark faithfully kept what he received rather than smoothing it over.

b: The Sabbath was rooted in creation, when God rested on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:11), and in rescue from slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:15). It was a gift of rest. Isaiah calls it ‘a delight’ (Isaiah 58:13).

Hebrews says a Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God, entered through faith in Christ (Hebrews 4:9–10). Christians gather on the first day of the week, the day of Jesus’ resurrection (Acts 20:7). How the fourth commandment applies to Christians is set out in the note on Matthew 12:1–8.

l.t: David receives the consecrated bread at Nob.
The Bread of the Presence, for Aaron and his sons.
Remember the Sabbath day: rooted in creation.
You may pluck heads of grain by hand.
Matthew adds the priests in the temple and ‘I desire mercy’.
Luke: the disciples rub the grain in their hands.
The next Sabbath conflict and the plot to kill Jesus.
A Sabbath rest remains for the people of God.

qs: What did the disciples do, and why did the Pharisees object?
What does ‘the Sabbath was made for man’ tell you about why God gave the Sabbath?
How could a regular day of rest and worship become a gift to you rather than a burden?

3.ctx: This is the last of the five conflict stories that began at 2:1, and it ends with a plot to kill Jesus (3:6). It happens on a Sabbath, in a synagogue. Jewish teaching allowed healing on the Sabbath when a life was in danger; English points out that this man’s life was not.
3.mean: Jesus goes into the synagogue again, and a man with a withered hand is there. Some of the people present are watching Jesus closely, not to learn from him but to catch him out. If he heals on the Sabbath, they will have a charge to bring against him. The man’s condition is not life-threatening, and Jesus could have told him to come back the next day. Instead he calls him to stand up where everyone can see. Then Jesus turns the question round. Instead of asking whether healing is allowed, he asks, ‘Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?’ Put that way, the answer is plain. God gave the Sabbath for good, and refusing help when you could give it is not a neutral choice. Yet they say nothing. They will not admit he is right, and they cannot show he is wrong. Mark lets you see Jesus’ face. He looks round at them ‘with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart’. He is angry because rules meant to honour God are being used to keep a suffering man in his trouble, and he is grieved because they cannot see it. Wesley summed it up: ‘Angry at the sin, grieved at the sinner.’ Then Jesus says to the man, ‘Stretch out your hand.’ He does not touch him; he only speaks. The man does what he is told, and his hand is restored. The reaction is shocking. The Pharisees walk out and begin plotting with the Herodians, people who supported the Herod family’s rule, ‘how they might kill Jesus’. Groups that normally distrusted each other join forces against him. On the day meant for doing good, Jesus restores a man’s body, and his opponents plan to destroy a life. His question has been answered by their own actions.
3.big: On the Sabbath Jesus restores a man’s withered hand, exposing hearts that care more for their rules than for a suffering man, and his opponents begin to plot his death.

vv.h: In order to accuse Jesus, they were watching to see if He would heal on the Sabbath
b: English explains that the verb suggests close, hostile watching, the way a suspect is watched. ‘Accuse’ is a legal word: the ESV Study Bible notes that they were gathering evidence for a formal case. Mark does not name the watchers until verse 6, where they turn out to be Pharisees. Wesley traced what was happening inside them: after being silenced so often, their pride, anger and shame ‘began now to ripen into malice’.

vv.h: Stand up among us
b: Cooper points out that this was not an emergency: Jesus could have waited a day. Instead he makes the healing deliberately public. The ESV Study Bible agrees that Jesus is not intimidated by his opponents. The man has been made into a test case, but to Jesus he is a person to be helped.

vv.h: Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?
b: English shows how Jesus argues on his opponents’ own ground, the law, and widens a narrow question (is healing allowed?) into a principle: when you are able to do good and refuse, you do harm. Calvin made the same point: sin is committed ‘not only by him who does any thing contrary to the Law, but also by him who neglects his duty.’ As Cooper puts it, ‘The one being tested became the tester.’
But they were silent. Wesley described them as ‘Being confounded, though not convinced.’ The ESV Study Bible sees their silence as a sign of the hardness of heart Mark names in the next verse.

vv.h: Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart
b: Matthew and Luke do not mention Jesus’ anger here (Matthew 12:13; Luke 6:10); Mark does. Calvin saw a model of holy anger: Jesus is grieved at their blindness and angry because malice has caused it. ‘This is the true moderation of zeal’, he wrote. He drew a further lesson: because Christ felt anger, emotions themselves are not sinful; ours go wrong through excess, his never did.

Why did their hardness matter so much? The ESV Study Bible explains that healing would not break the Old Testament law, but it would break the Pharisees’ added tradition, which had lost sight of the law’s purpose: to love God and your neighbour (12:29–31).

vv.h: Stretch out your hand
b: English notes that the man ‘obeys the command given, joins in the healing process’. He is asked to do the very thing he cannot do, and he does it on Jesus’ word. Calvin pointed out that the critics should have asked whether restoring a hand by a single word was the work of God or of a man.

vv.h: the Pharisees went out and began plotting with the Herodians how they might kill Jesus
b: The Pharisees cared intensely about keeping God’s law; the Herodians backed the Herod family, who ruled with Rome’s approval (see History). Calvin said the Pharisees ‘regarded the Herodians with the fiercest hatred’, and Wesley called the two groups ‘as bitter as they usually were against each other’. Hostility to Jesus brought them together; the ESV Study Bible compares the rulers who gather ‘against His Anointed One’ in Psalm 2:2. The same two groups appear together again in 12:13, trying to trap Jesus over taxes, and the leaders’ plan to kill him resurfaces in 14:1.

In the New Testament the Herodians appear at Mark 3:6, Mark 12:13 and Matthew 22:16, each time alongside the Pharisees. Who exactly they were is disputed. The Lexham Bible Dictionary describes them as a Jewish party that sympathised with the Herod family’s rule, and therefore with Rome, and reports two suggestions: that they were courtiers, servants and officials of Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee (Meier), or people who thought Herod or one of his sons was the Messiah (Bennett). English and the ESV Study Bible take them as supporters of Herod Antipas. The source read gives no majority view.

b: God gave the Sabbath as a day of rest and blessing (Exodus 20:8–11). Jesus has just called himself ‘Lord even of the Sabbath’ (2:28); here he shows what the Lord of the Sabbath does with it. John records another Sabbath healing that led straight to a plan to kill Jesus (John 5:16–18).

The ESV Study Bible points to Psalm 2, where rulers gather ‘against the LORD and against His Anointed One’. The first Christians saw the same psalm fulfilled when Herod and Pilate joined against Jesus (Acts 4:25–27).

l.t: Matthew: a sheep in a pit on the Sabbath.
Luke: it was his right hand.
Rulers gather against the LORD’s Anointed.
Another Sabbath healing, another plot.
A bent woman healed on the Sabbath.
Pharisees and Herodians together again.
The heart of the law: love God and neighbour.
Psalm 2 and the plot against Jesus.

qs: What question did Jesus ask in the synagogue, and how did the people respond?
Why does Jesus’ question make silence a kind of answer?
Where might your own rules or habits stop you from doing good for someone who needs help?

3.ctx: After the plot of 3:6, Jesus leaves the synagogue for the shore of the Sea of Galilee. People come from Galilee and Judea, from Jerusalem, from Idumea in the far south, from east of the Jordan and from around Tyre and Sidon on the coast to the north-west.
3.mean: The religious leaders have turned against Jesus, but ordinary people are flocking to him. Mark gives a long list of places to show how far the news has spread: from Galilee where Jesus lives, south to Judea, Jerusalem and Idumea, east beyond the Jordan, and north to the coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon. People have heard ‘what great things He was doing’ and they come to see for themselves. The pressure is so great that Jesus asks his disciples to keep a boat ready, so that he can step away from the shore if the crowd begins to crush him. So many have been healed that the sick are pushing forward just to touch him. It is a picture of overwhelming need and overwhelming power. Then something strange happens. Whenever unclean spirits see him, they fall down in front of him and shout, ‘You are the Son of God!’ What they say is true; it is exactly what Mark announced in his first verse (1:1). Yet Jesus sternly orders them not to make him known. Why silence a true statement? Mark does not explain, and readers have given different answers (see the history note on the ‘messianic secret’ at Mark 1:40). Calvin thought Jesus refused to accept witnesses like these, and that he chose to be revealed gradually, at the time his Father had set. The ESV Study Bible adds that the spirits’ intent was evil even when their words were true, and that announcing his identity too soon would cause misunderstanding. English points out that crowds drawn by healing and spectacle could easily attach the title ‘Son of God’ to the wrong thing. Who Jesus really is will be shown most clearly at the cross, where a Roman centurion, not a demon, will say, ‘Truly this man was the Son of God!’ (15:39). Being impressed by Jesus is not yet the same as following him.
3.big: Huge crowds from every region come to Jesus for healing, and the unclean spirits recognise him as the Son of God, but he silences them.

vv.h: So Jesus withdrew with His disciples to the sea
b: Matthew links this withdrawal with the plot (Matthew 12:14–15). Calvin insisted it was not fear: the time his Father had appointed for him to die had not yet come (John 7:30). Cooper says the same: ‘It was not yet his time’. English adds that Mark presents the move as an extension of the ministry rather than an escape. Jesus leaves the synagogue, where the learned oppose him, and goes where ordinary people receive him gladly.

vv.h: Jerusalem, Idumea, the region beyond the Jordan, and the vicinity of Tyre and Sidon
b: The ESV Study Bible notes that all these regions had belonged to Israel in the time of the judges, and that descendants of the twelve tribes had resettled there after the exile to Babylon. Wesley thought those from Tyre and Sidon were ‘The Israelites who lived in those coasts’. Cooper takes the list to mean that his reputation had reached Gentile regions too. Either way, people from almost every direction are now coming to him.

vv.h: to have a boat ready for Him so that the crowd would not crush Him
b: Cooper calls the boat simple wisdom: being at the centre of a huge crowd is dangerous. The same boat becomes Jesus’ pulpit in 4:1. The ESV Study Bible observes that Jesus’ popularity grew mainly from his healings and exorcisms, but his chief aim was to teach about the kingdom of God and call people to it (1:14–15). Cooper adds a warning: many wanted a miracle worker rather than a Lord.

vv.h: You are the Son of God!
b: They ‘fell down before Him’: the evil spirits recognise that he has authority over them. Calvin wrote that ‘divine power extorted from the devils this confession’. Cooper reports two readings of the title on their lips: some take it in its fullest sense, others as meaning simply someone close to God; he thinks the spirits knew who Jesus was and what he meant for their kingdom.

vv.h: But He warned them sternly not to make Him known
b: Wesley gave two reasons: ‘It was not the time: nor were they fit preachers.’ The ESV Study Bible says their intent was evil even when their words were true, and early disclosure would lead to misunderstanding. English writes that ‘faith needs firmer ground than that’. These are the commentators’ explanations; scholars still debate why Mark records so many commands to silence (see the history note at Mark 1:40).

Matthew sees in Jesus’ quietness the fulfilment of Isaiah’s servant who ‘will not quarrel or cry out’ (Matthew 12:17–21, quoting Isaiah 42:1–4). Mark does not quote Isaiah here, but his picture is the same: great power, with no grab for fame.

‘Son of God’ runs through Mark from the first verse (1:1) through the Father’s voice at the baptism (1:11) and the transfiguration (9:7) to the centurion at the cross (15:39). The demons say it first; a human being says it last, at the foot of the cross.

l.t: Matthew: Isaiah’s gentle servant.
Luke: power was going out from him.
The servant who will not cry out.
An earlier spirit silenced.
He would not let the demons speak.
Another spirit names the Son of the Most High God.
The centurion: truly the Son of God.
Even the demons believe, and shudder.

qs: Where did the crowds come from, and what were they looking for?
Why might Jesus refuse a true statement about himself when it came from evil spirits?
What is the difference between being impressed by Jesus and following him?

3.ctx: Jesus has a growing crowd of followers and a growing number of enemies. Luke records that he spent the night before this in prayer (Luke 6:12). Mark gives the names of the Twelve, the inner group whom Jesus will later send out (6:7–13).
3.mean: Jesus goes up on the mountain and calls ‘those He wanted’. The choice is his. These men are not volunteers who applied, and they are not chosen for being better than others: the list ends with Judas. They answer by coming to him. From those who come, Jesus appoints twelve. Mark gives their purpose in a few words, and the order matters. First, they are ‘to accompany Him’: to be with Jesus, to watch him, to listen to him and to learn from him. Only then are they to be sent out, to preach and to have authority to drive out demons. Being with Jesus comes before working for him. ‘Apostle’ means someone who is sent, a messenger who carries the authority of the one who sent him. The number twelve is no accident. Israel had twelve tribes, and the ESV Study Bible notes that the Twelve probably represent them: Jesus is gathering a renewed people of God around himself. Revelation pictures the names of the twelve apostles on the foundations of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:14). Then Mark lists them. Some names come with nicknames. Simon becomes Peter, which means rock. James and John become ‘Sons of Thunder’, which may describe their fiery temper (Luke 9:54) or, as Calvin and Wesley thought, the power of their later preaching. Matthew the tax collector, who had worked for the system that served Rome, sits beside Simon the Zealot, whose title links him with zeal for Israel; Cooper notes how far apart the two were in politics. Last comes ‘Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus’. English, following Anderson, points out that a list beginning with Peter, who denied Jesus, and ending with Judas, who betrayed him, shows these were not men who were perfect from the start. Calvin saw in the call nothing but ‘the unmixed grace of Christ’. Jesus still calls ordinary, flawed people, and he still wants them with him before he sends them.
3.big: Jesus chooses twelve ordinary men to be with him and to be sent out with his message and authority, forming the core of a renewed people of God.

vv.h: called for those He wanted, and they came to Him
b: English finds three marks of discipleship here: separation (going up the mountain, away from ordinary life), Jesus’ initiative (he calls whom he wants) and an immediate response (they came). Calvin drew a theological lesson: ‘to the unmixed grace of Christ, and not to any excellence of their own’ they owed their place; Judas proves it was not merit. Wesley drew a line: as to people’s eternal states God always acts as just and merciful, but in other matters, such as this choice, ‘he seems to us to act as a mere sovereign’.

vv.h: He appointed twelve of them, whom He designated as apostles, to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach
b: The ESV Study Bible sets out a twofold task: to be with him, which is the heart of discipleship, and to be sent out, which gives ‘apostle’ its sense of those who are sent out. Cooper defines an apostle as ‘one who is sent with the authority of another’. English calls their work ‘witnessing, proclaiming, setting people free’, and adds that the faith and commitment expected of them is expected of every disciple.

Some early manuscripts do not include the words ‘whom He designated as apostles’ here; Luke has them (Luke 6:13). Calvin thought this calling prepared them for a commission they would receive later, when Jesus sent them out (6:7–13).

vv.h: Simon (whom He named Peter)
b: Peter means rock (Greek petros). English notes that ‘Rock-like’ hardly describes Peter’s whole record in the New Testament, yet he became the rallying point for the others, especially after Pentecost. Peter is named first in every list of the apostles. What Peter’s place means for the church is discussed at Matthew 10:1–4 and Matthew 16:18.

vv.h: Boanerges, meaning “Sons of Thunder”
b: Mark translates the Aramaic for his readers. Cooper and English link the nickname with the brothers’ fiery temper, seen when they wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village (Luke 9:54). Calvin and Wesley read it of their future preaching; Calvin said Christ named them so ‘that they might thunder throughout the whole world’.

vv.h: Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot
b: Cooper reports that most scholars identify Bartholomew with the Nathanael of John 1:45–49, and thinks Thaddaeus is probably the ‘Judas son of James’ of Luke 6:16. The BSB notes that the Greek calls Simon ‘the Cananean’, which Luke renders ‘the Zealot’ (Luke 6:15). Cooper, following Barbieri, remarks that Simon the Zealot and Matthew the tax collector stood miles apart politically, yet followed the same Lord.

vv.h: and Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus
b: Mark does not explain ‘Iscariot’. Cooper gives the traditional derivation, man from Kerioth, a town in Judah, and mentions another suggestion (Stock’s); neither is certain. Why choose Judas at all? Calvin answered that Jesus meant to warn the church in advance, so that believers would not be shaken when people in high places fall away. The ESV Study Bible notes that Judas was called to be with Jesus and to proclaim, heal and drive out demons; he was loved and warned by Jesus, but not trusted (John 2:24; 6:64, 70).
Jesus himself tells the disciples, ‘You did not choose Me, but I chose you’ (John 15:16). Mark’s ‘those He wanted’ makes the same point at the start.

After Judas’s death the eleven chose Matthias to restore the number to twelve (Acts 1:15–26), which shows how much the number mattered to them. The heavenly city has ‘twelve foundations bearing the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb’ (Revelation 21:14).

l.t: Matthew: the Twelve sent with authority.
Luke: a night of prayer first.
The eleven in the upper room.
The Twelve sent out two by two.
You did not choose Me, but I chose you.
James and John and the fire from heaven.
One of you is a devil.
The twelve apostles of the Lamb.

qs: What two things did Jesus appoint the Twelve to do, and in what order?
Why might Jesus have chosen men as different as Matthew the tax collector and Simon the Zealot?
What would it look like for you to spend time ‘with Jesus’ before trying to work for him?

3.ctx: Mark wraps one story inside another: Jesus’ family set out to fetch him (3:20–21) and arrive at the end (3:31–35); in between come the scribes from Jerusalem (3:22–30). English notes that Mark sets the two kinds of unbelief side by side.
3.mean: Jesus is back at home, and the crowds are so thick that he and his disciples cannot even eat. When his family hear about it, they set out ‘to take custody of Him’, the word used for seizing someone, because they think he is ‘out of His mind’. They are worried for him, perhaps for the family too, but they do not understand him. Then a more serious charge arrives. Scribes have come all the way from Jerusalem, the centre of religious authority. They cannot deny that Jesus drives out demons; everyone has seen it. So they explain it another way: he is possessed by Beelzebul, and he drives out demons by the power of the prince of demons. The ESV Study Bible notes that they implicitly admit his ‘undeniable powers’, but call them satanic. Jesus answers with two pictures. First, a divided kingdom or household cannot stand. If Satan were driving out his own demons, he would be at war with himself, and his rule would be finished. The accusation does not make sense. Second, nobody can break into a strong man’s house and carry off his goods unless he first ties up the strong man. Satan is the strong man; the people he holds captive are his goods. If Jesus is setting them free, it is because someone stronger has come and overpowered Satan. Isaiah had asked whether captives could be rescued from a tyrant, and God had promised that they would be (Isaiah 49:24–25). Jesus is that stronger one. English adds a realistic note: in Mark’s day, as in ours, Satan ‘might be a defeated foe but he was not yet a powerless one’. The same question faces every reader. Seeing what Jesus does, you cannot stay neutral: either his power is evil, or God’s rule has arrived in him. His family think he is mad; the scribes think he is in league with the devil. Mark wants you to see that he is the stronger one, come to set captives free.
3.big: Accused of driving out demons by Satan’s power, Jesus shows that the charge is absurd and that he is the stronger one who has bound Satan and is setting his captives free.

vv.h: Then Jesus went home
b: Literally He comes to a house (BSB footnote). The ESV Study Bible takes it to be the place where he stayed in Capernaum (compare 2:1). Wesley explains the phrase about eating as not being able ‘to take any subsistence’.

vv.h: When His family heard about this, they went out to take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”
b: Only Mark tells this part. English notes that Mark’s verb is used for taking someone by the hand or for arresting them, and he thinks there is strong evidence that the ones saying ‘He is out of His mind’ were the family themselves. Wesley took ‘His relations’ to be ‘His mother and his brethren, ver. 31’, and Calvin wrote that they meant ‘to bind him as if he had been a madman’. Cooper suggests they were concerned for the family name and for his safety. John later says that ‘even His own brothers did not believe in Him’ (John 7:5). The ESV Study Bible adds that some of his brothers did later come to faith (it points to 1 Corinthians 9:5; compare Acts 1:14).

vv.h: the scribes who had come down from Jerusalem
b: English notes that Jesus’ fame, and the opposition to him, have now reached Jerusalem, where the final contest will take place. Wesley commented sharply: ‘How easily may a man of learning elude the strongest proof of a work of God!’ Cooper notes that the verb is in a tense that suggests they kept on saying it.

vv.h: He is possessed by Beelzebul
b: Beelzebul comes from the name of a god worshipped at the Philistine city of Ekron. In 2 Kings 1:2 King Ahaziah consults ‘Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron’. The Lexham Bible Dictionary explains that Baal-zebub (lord of the flies) is probably a mocking twist on Baal-zebul (prince Baal), though the meaning is uncertain (see History). By Jesus’ time the name had come to stand for Satan or a chief demon. English notes that Jesus answers as though Beelzebul and Satan are one, and Matthew and Luke treat them that way too.

vv.h: How can Satan drive out Satan?
b: Mark says Jesus spoke ‘in parables’, here meaning picture-sayings. Calvin noted that Jesus uses a common proverb as a reasonable argument rather than a strict proof, and that it works because everyone could see that his exorcisms restored people ‘sound and whole’ to God. Satan does not set his own prisoners free.

vv.h: no one can enter a strong man’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man
b: Isaiah asked, ‘Can the plunder be snatched from the mighty?’ and God answered that ‘the plunder of the tyrant will be retrieved’ (Isaiah 49:24–25). Calvin explained that people held by Satan cannot free themselves, and Satan ‘will never yield of his own accord’, so a stronger one had to come from heaven. Jesus’ victory, begun in the wilderness (1:12–13) and shown in every exorcism, is won decisively at the cross (Colossians 2:15).

The form ‘Baal-zebub’ appears in 2 Kings 1:2–16 as the god of the Philistine city of Ekron. Its meaning is uncertain. The Lexham Bible Dictionary (Charles Meeks) thinks it likely that Baal-zebub (lord of the flies) is a deliberate mockery of Baal-zebul (prince Baal), the god actually worshipped at Ekron; others read the fly as a neutral description (Tångberg), or suggest Baal, the Flame (Fensham) or Baal of the heavens (Gaston). The Gospels’ form, Beelzebul, may echo a word for house or dwelling, which fits Jesus’ talk of a house divided and a strong man’s house (MacLaurin); English takes Lord of the dwelling as the most likely meaning. In the Testament of Solomon, a pseudepigraphal writing (one written under a famous name), Beelzebul is called the ‘Prince of Demons’, as in the scribes’ charge.

b: Luke’s version has Jesus say he drives out demons ‘by the finger of God’ (Luke 11:20), the words Pharaoh’s magicians used about the plagues (Exodus 8:19). Matthew has ‘by the Spirit of God’ (Matthew 12:28). Either way, the exorcisms show that God’s kingdom has arrived.
John sums up why Jesus came: ‘to destroy the works of the devil’ (1 John 3:8). Paul says that at the cross Christ ‘disarmed the powers and authorities’ (Colossians 2:15).

Luke: by the finger of God.
The tyrant’s plunder retrieved.
Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.
This is the finger of God.
His brothers did not believe in him.
The powers disarmed at the cross.

How do Jesus’ two pictures, the divided house and the strong man, answer the scribes?

3.ctx: Jesus is still answering the scribes from Jerusalem, who have said that his power over demons comes from Satan (3:22). Mark tells you why he spoke these words: ‘because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit”’ (3:30).
3.mean: These are some of the most serious words Jesus ever spoke, and they begin with a great promise. ‘Truly I tell you,’ he says, a phrase that marks what follows as solemn and certain: ‘the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter.’ No sin is too great for God’s forgiveness, and no words spoken against him are beyond his mercy. The ESV Study Bible sees here the reach of Jesus’ coming death, which he will describe as ‘a ransom for many’ (10:45). Then comes the warning: ‘whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.’ What is this sin? Mark answers in the next sentence. Jesus said this ‘because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”’ The scribes had seen captives set free by the Spirit of God, and they called it the work of the devil. They were not asking honest questions or struggling with doubt. As English puts it, ‘in the presence of God’s grace in action, they have not only rejected it but ascribed it to the devil.’ Why can this not be forgiven? English answers that it is not because God’s mercy runs out: there is no forgiveness ‘because such an attitude is incapable of seeking it.’ If you call the Healer a destroyer, you will not come to him to be healed. Christians have understood the sin in slightly different ways (see Where readings differ). Cooper draws out a pastoral point: someone who is troubled by the fear of having committed it, and wants God’s forgiveness, is turning towards God, not away from him. He notes that this is one of the most common worries Christians have, and that Jesus never turns away anyone who comes to him with a repentant heart. The warning is real, and it is aimed at hardened opposition to God’s work. The promise is just as real, and it is for everyone who will receive it.
3.big: Jesus promises forgiveness for all sins and blasphemies, but warns that calling the Holy Spirit’s work in him the work of the devil shuts the door on forgiveness.

vv.h: Truly I tell you
b: Literally Amen, I say to you. English, citing Cranfield, explains that with these words Jesus solemnly guarantees the truth of what follows. Mark uses the phrase here for the first time; Jesus will use it often. Cooper calls it a way of saying: what comes next is of great importance, so pay attention.

vv.h: the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter
b: Cooper calls this ‘a great promise ... linked with a solemn warning’. The ESV Study Bible links it with Jesus’ substitutionary death (10:45). Matthew and Luke include a saying that even ‘a word against the Son of Man’ can be forgiven (Matthew 12:32; Luke 12:10). Calvin noted that Paul, who had once been a blasphemer, received mercy because he acted ‘in ignorance and unbelief’ (1 Timothy 1:13).

vv.h: whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin
b: Blasphemy means speaking against God, insulting or slandering him. Here it is directed against the Holy Spirit, by whose power Jesus was driving out demons (compare Matthew 12:28). Matthew has ‘either in this age or in the one to come’ (Matthew 12:32); Calvin said Mark’s ‘eternal’ explains Matthew’s words. Wesley took Matthew’s phrase as a Jewish expression for something that would never happen.

Cooper writes, ‘Of all the things that Christians worry about, this is one of the most common.’ He repeats a common saying, ‘If you are worried about it, you have not done it’, and adds that Jesus never turns away anyone who asks for forgiveness with a repentant heart. English makes a similar point: there is no forgiveness here ‘because such an attitude is incapable of seeking it.’

vv.h: Jesus made this statement because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”
b: Mark ties the warning to the scribes’ words. Commenting on Matthew 12:31, Wesley thought nothing in the Bible was plainer: the sin is ‘neither more nor less than the ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil, which Christ wrought by the power of the Holy Ghost.’ Cooper notes that ‘were saying’ is in a tense that suggests repeated, settled speech: ‘It does not refer to an act so much as it refers to a steady disposition against God.’ English wonders whether Jesus meant that they had not yet reached the point of no return, and was warning them against hardening further.

3.diff: What exactly is the sin against the Holy Spirit? (1) The specific sin of the scribes. Wesley held that it is ‘the ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil, which Christ wrought by the power of the Holy Ghost’, which is what the scribes did. (2) Deliberate slander of what you know to be God’s work. Calvin argued that only those blaspheme the Spirit ‘who slander his gifts and power, contrary to the conviction of their own mind’; unlike Paul, they cannot plead ignorance. In keeping with Reformed teaching, he added that it is ‘a token of reprobation’ (a sign that God has finally given a person up) and that ‘he who has been truly regenerated by the Spirit cannot possibly fall into so horrid a crime’ (that is, no one truly born again can commit it). (3) A settled, persistent stance. English, Cooper and the ESV Study Bible stress the continuing hostility: the ESV Study Bible describes a person who ‘persistently attributes to Satan what is accomplished by the power of God’, and English suggests Jesus may have been warning the scribes before they reached that point. These readings overlap. Cooper adds the pastoral point that someone who is worried about having committed this sin has not done so, and English says that there is no forgiveness because the attitude is ‘incapable of seeking it.’

b: Isaiah describes Israel in the wilderness: ‘they rebelled and grieved His Holy Spirit’ (Isaiah 63:10). Stephen accused the council of always resisting the Holy Spirit (Acts 7:51).

Hebrews contains other serious warnings about turning away after receiving the light (Hebrews 6:4–6; 10:26–29). Christians read those passages in different ways, but they share the same aim as Jesus’ words here: to warn against hardening your heart while there is still time.

l.t: Matthew: neither in this age nor the next.
Luke: in a later setting.
A ransom for many.
Paul the blasphemer shown mercy.
They grieved His Holy Spirit.
Always resisting the Holy Spirit.
A warning about falling away.
If we confess, he forgives.

qs: Why, according to Mark, did Jesus speak these words?
How can Jesus say both that all sins will be forgiven and that one will not?
How does this passage comfort someone who is afraid they are beyond God’s forgiveness?

3.ctx: This closes the story that began at 3:20–21, when Jesus’ family set out to take him home. English notes that Nazareth was some twenty miles away, and that this passage and 6:3 are the only places where Mark refers directly to Mary.
3.mean: Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive at last. They stand outside and send someone in to call him. The crowd is sitting around him, and someone passes on the message: ‘Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You.’ English suggests that the crowd expected Jesus either to go out to them or to make room for them to come in. Instead he asks a startling question: ‘Who are My mother and My brothers?’ Then he looks at the people sitting in a circle around him, listening to him, and says, ‘Here are My mother and My brothers! For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.’ Notice where everyone is. The family Mark has just told you thought Jesus was ‘out of His mind’ (3:21) stand outside. The people who have come to hear him sit inside, around him. Jesus is not rejecting his family. He cared for his mother to the very end, giving her into the care of his beloved disciple from the cross (John 19:26–27), and later his mother and brothers are found praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14). But he is saying that there is a family that goes deeper than blood: everyone who does God’s will. Calvin wrote that there is ‘no tie of relationship more sacred than spiritual relationship’. Doing God’s will does not mean earning a place by perfect obedience. Calvin explained that it means trusting God and so beginning to obey him, which is the mark of belonging. There is great comfort here. Anyone, man or woman, can belong to Jesus’ family, and Jesus is not ashamed to call them his brothers and sisters (Hebrews 2:11). For someone whose own family rejects their faith, English writes, ‘Your family is much, much larger than that!’ There is challenge too: even the closest human ties must not come before following Jesus. Later Jesus promises that anyone who leaves family for his sake will receive ‘a hundredfold’ in brothers, sisters and mothers in this life (10:29–30).
3.big: Jesus’ true family is everyone who does the will of God, a family deeper than blood that is open to all.

vv.h: Jesus’ mother and brothers came and stood outside
b: Why had they come? Mark has already told you that the family thought he was out of his mind (3:21). Calvin, by contrast, thought they were moved by anxiety for him or by ‘pious zeal’, and rejected the accusation of Ambrose and Chrysostom that Mary was ambitious. English pictures Mary as anxious for her son, perhaps by now without Joseph, whose absence from these scenes suggests to English that he had died; he says this neither weakens belief in the virgin birth nor makes her unworthy. Who Jesus’ ‘brothers’ were is discussed below (Where readings differ).

vv.h: Your mother and brothers are outside, asking for You
b: Some manuscripts add ‘and Your sisters’ (BSB footnote). Mark 6:3 mentions his sisters and names four brothers: James, Joses, Judas and Simon. The ESV Study Bible suggests that the family ‘seeking’ him here were trying to ‘seize’ him, as in 3:21.

vv.h: Who are My mother and My brothers?
b: Cooper insists this is not meant harshly: Jesus’ aim ‘was not to destroy family’, but family must be seen in the light of higher priorities. Calvin thought the words were meant ‘to reprove Mary’s eagerness’ in interrupting his teaching. English warns that the passage gives no excuse for groups that pull people away from their families: God placed us in families, and the New Testament teaches their importance.

vv.h: Looking at those seated in a circle around Him
b: Mark often notes where Jesus looks (3:5; 10:23). Cooper points out that those sitting around him were disciples, while the scribes of the previous scene were certainly not at his feet. Wesley imagined him looking round ‘With the utmost sweetness’.

vv.h: For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother
b: Jesus adds ‘sister’, though only brothers were mentioned: the family is open to women and men alike. The ESV Study Bible compares Psalm 22:22, quoted in Hebrews 2:11–12, where the Messiah calls God’s people his brothers. Calvin explained that ‘does the will of God’ does not mean keeping the law perfectly but commends faith, the source of obedience (John 6:40). Yet Christ ‘discharged his lawful duties towards relatives’, so believers must still honour their families.

3.diff: Who were Jesus’ ‘brothers’ and ‘sisters’? The Lexham Bible Dictionary (Charles Meeks, following Brashler and Bauckham) sets out three main views. (1) Children of Mary and Joseph, born after Jesus. This takes the Greek adelphos in its ordinary sense of brother. The dictionary associates it with Tertullian and with the majority of Protestants; English holds it (‘Mark means natural brother to Jesus, borne by Mary’), and the ESV Study Bible speaks of Jesus’ ‘half brothers’. (2) Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. A popular view among the church fathers, found in the second-century Protevangelium of James and defended by Epiphanius. (3) Cousins or other close relatives. Jerome argued that they were sons of another Mary, the wife of Clopas (compare Mark 15:40; John 19:25). According to the dictionary (citing John P. Meier), after Jerome this became the common view in Catholicism and among early Protestants. Calvin held that ‘brothers’ here means relatives, after ‘the Hebrew idiom’, and Wesley took them as ‘his kinsmen’, sons of Mary the wife of Clopas. The Catholic Church teaches that Mary remained a virgin and that these are ‘close relations of Jesus, according to an Old Testament expression’ (Catechism 500). The Orthodox Church calls Mary ‘ever-virgin’, teaching that she ‘remained and remains a virgin before the birth, during the birth, and after the birth of the Saviour’ (Longer Catechism, question 186); that answer concerns Mary’s virginity and does not say who the brothers were. Calvin, on Matthew 1:25, held that ‘no just and well-grounded inference can be drawn’ from Matthew’s ‘until’ about what happened after Jesus’ birth. The passage itself does not settle the question; its point is the new family Jesus is forming.

b: Psalm 22, a psalm Jesus prayed from the cross, ends with praise: ‘I will proclaim Your name to my brothers’ (Psalm 22:22). Hebrews applies it to Jesus, who ‘is not ashamed to call them brothers’ (Hebrews 2:11–12).

Jesus’ family did not stay outside for ever. After the resurrection Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), and his mother and brothers joined the disciples in prayer (Acts 1:14). James became a leader of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9; Acts 15:13).

l.t: Matthew: whoever does the will of My Father.
Luke: those who hear the word and carry it out.
Blessed rather are those who hear and obey.
His brothers did not believe in him.
Jesus entrusts his mother to the disciple.
Mary and his brothers at prayer.
A hundredfold brothers, sisters and mothers.
Not ashamed to call them brothers.

qs: Who was standing outside, and who was sitting around Jesus?
What does Jesus mean by doing ‘the will of God’, and why does that make someone his family?
How could the church be a real family to someone whose own family rejects their faith?

4.ctx: Mark now gathers several of Jesus’ parables into one section (4:1–34), framed by notes about his teaching (4:1–2, 33–34). Jesus teaches from a boat on the Sea of Galilee while the crowd stands on the shore. Farmers sowed by hand, scattering seed across the field.
4.mean: The crowd is so large that Jesus gets into a boat and teaches from the water while the people line the shore. He begins with one word: ‘Listen!’ Then he tells a story everyone there would recognise. A farmer goes out and scatters seed by hand. Some falls on the hard path that runs along the field, and birds eat it straight away. Some falls on rocky ground, where a thin layer of soil covers the rock. It springs up fast in the shallow soil, but when the sun beats down the young plants wither, because they have no roots. Some falls among thorns, which grow up with it and choke it, so it produces nothing. And some falls on good soil, where it grows and produces a crop: thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was sown. Jesus ends with a challenge: ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’ He does not explain the story yet; he will do that for his disciples in 4:13–20. For now the crowd is left to think. What is the story about? Notice what makes the difference. The farmer is the same throughout, and so is the seed. What differs is the ground. English says the receptivity of the ground determines the harvest. Notice too how the story ends. Three quarters of the story is about loss, but the last part is about a harvest far larger than an ordinary one. The ESV Study Bible notes that typical yields were much smaller, and links a hundredfold with God’s blessing (Genesis 26:12). Jesus is teaching that the word of God will meet much failure and opposition, as he himself was meeting it. Yet where it is truly received it produces an abundance far beyond what anyone could expect. The question ‘Listen!’ puts to every hearer is simple: what kind of ground am I?
4.big: In the parable of the sower Jesus shows that God’s word meets different kinds of hearers, and that where it is truly received it produces an astonishing harvest.

vv.h: He got into a boat and sat in it
b: This may be the boat the disciples kept ready in 3:9. Cooper notes that teachers usually sat to teach, and that teaching from the water let more people see and hear. Wesley thought Jesus later crossed the lake in this same vessel (4:36).

vv.h: He taught them many things in parables
b: A parable is a picture or story from everyday life that shows a spiritual truth. Cooper explains the Greek as to throw alongside: a familiar thing is set beside God’s truth to throw light on it. Wesley wrote that a parable can be any instructive speech ‘wherein spiritual things are explained and illustrated by natural’. English says Jesus’ parables call for ‘serious, persistent, perceptive faith’: the hearer has to work at them. ‘Many things’ reminds you that Mark gives only a selection (4:33).

vv.h: Listen! A farmer went out to sow his seed
b: Wesley thought Jesus probably said ‘Listen!’ in a loud voice to still the noise of the crowd; Cooper calls it an invitation to the hearers to take part in the story. The ESV Study Bible explains that the sower scattered the seed without ploughing the ground first, so it fell on ground that had not been prepared for it.

vv.h: rocky ground ... thorns
b: Cooper explains that farmers cleared stones from their fields but could never get them all, and that seed in a thin layer of soil over rock would shoot up quickly and then die in the heat. Thorns and weeds grew alongside the crop and starved it. Farmers in the crowd would have recognised all four kinds of ground.

vv.h: one bearing thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold
b: The ESV Study Bible says typical yields ‘ranged from about fivefold to fifteenfold’, so a tenfold return was a good crop, though some historical reports speak of up to a hundredfold. When Isaac sowed and reaped a hundredfold, Genesis says, ‘the LORD blessed him’ (Genesis 26:12). Calvin thought the figure was ‘not hyperbolical’, citing historians who reported such fertility in some lands. Either way, the point is an abundant harvest.

vv.h: He who has ears to hear, let him hear
b: Everyone in the crowd had ears; not everyone would truly hear. The ESV Study Bible says that real hearing means giving up proud self-reliance and submitting to God. Calvin added that ‘it is the Lord who pierces the ears’, citing Psalm 40 (in the BSB, ‘my ears You have opened’, Psalm 40:6). Cooper notes that the saying turns the parable into a question for each hearer: what kind of soil am I for the word of God?

Isaiah compares God’s word to rain that waters the earth and makes it sprout; God says his word ‘will not return to Me empty’ (Isaiah 55:11). The sower parable shares that confidence: not every seed bears fruit, but the word will produce its harvest.
Jesus explains the parable in 4:13–20. Paul uses the same picture of sowing and growth for his own ministry: ‘I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow’ (1 Corinthians 3:6).

l.t: Matthew: the same parable by the sea.
Luke: crowds from town after town.
God’s word will not return empty.
Isaac reaps a hundredfold.
Do not sow among thorns.
God gives the growth.
The gospel bearing fruit and growing.

qs: What happens to the seed on each of the four kinds of ground?
Why do you think Jesus told the story without explaining it to the crowd?
Which kind of ground best describes how you receive God’s word at the moment, and why?
