4.ctx: Later, away from the crowd, the Twelve and others who follow Jesus ask him about the parable. His answer quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, where God sends Isaiah to a people who will hear his message but not take it in. English calls this passage ‘amongst the most difficult passages in the New Testament’.
4.mean: When the crowd has gone, the Twelve and the others around Jesus ask him about the parables. His answer is surprising. ‘The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables.’ In the Bible a ‘mystery’ is not a puzzle to be solved by cleverness. It is something hidden until God chooses to reveal it. Here the mystery is that God’s kingdom has arrived in Jesus himself, the lowly teacher from Nazareth. The disciples have not worked this out by being cleverer than others; it ‘has been given’ to them. They are ‘inside’ because they have come to Jesus and stayed with him (3:14, 34). Others stand ‘outside’, like Jesus’ family in 3:31. For them, Jesus says, everything comes ‘in parables’, and he quotes Isaiah: ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’ When God called Isaiah, he warned him that the people would refuse to listen, and that his preaching would harden them further. Jesus’ ministry repeats that pattern. The same parable that opens the eyes of someone who comes to Jesus with questions leaves the person who stands back none the wiser. Cooper calls parables spiritual tests: they hide the truth from those who do not seek it and reveal it to those who do. The hardest words are ‘so that’. Does Jesus speak in parables in order to keep people from understanding, or is he describing what happens when they refuse? Christians have answered in different ways (see Where readings differ). Calvin, Wesley, English and Cooper each hold the outsiders responsible for their refusal, and the ESV Study Bible adds that there is still room for repentance. Even the disciples will struggle to understand (4:13). The invitation stands: come to Jesus and ask, as the disciples did.
4.big: The secret of God’s kingdom is given to those who come to Jesus, while those who stay outside hear the parables without understanding, as Isaiah foretold.

vv.h: As soon as Jesus was alone with the Twelve and those around Him
b: Notice that more than the Twelve are present. The ESV Study Bible notes that these followers receive insight into the parables; English praises them for coming to Jesus with their questions. Wesley explains ‘alone’ as ‘retired apart from the multitude’.

vv.h: The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you
b: English explains that the ‘mystery’ is not borrowed from the pagan mystery religions but is an Old Testament idea: something hidden until God reveals it, which cannot otherwise be known. Citing Cranfield, he identifies the secret of the kingdom with the secret of who Jesus is. The ESV Study Bible describes it as the nature of God’s rule over individuals and over his community. ‘Has been given’ points to God as the giver; Cooper says the disciples received it ‘not because of their superior spiritual state, but because the Lord Jesus had chosen them’.

vv.h: but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables
b: Wesley wrote that the Jews called the Gentiles ‘without’, and that Jesus here so ‘terms all obstinate unbelievers’. Cooper thinks the outsiders are mainly the religious leaders who had just accused Jesus of working by Beelzebul (3:22). The ESV Study Bible defines them as those who do not (yet) belong to Jesus’ community: the ‘yet’ leaves the door open.

vv.h: so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’
b: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10; English thinks Mark’s form comes from the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament (the BSB footnote also points to it). In Isaiah’s own words God says, ‘Be ever hearing, but never understanding; be ever seeing, but never perceiving’, and the people might ‘turn and be healed’. Mark has ‘be forgiven’, which Calvin said names the cause and source of the healing.

English admits the difficulty: some suggest ‘with the result that’ instead of ‘so that’, which ‘would certainly be easier!’, and Matthew and Luke soften it, ‘but sharp it remains’. The ESV Study Bible reads it as a prophetic warning to Gentiles and Jews alike, with ‘still room for repentance’. Calvin said God’s word is not itself the cause of blindness but becomes so ‘by accident’, as bright sunlight dazzles weak eyes.

4.diff: Why do some understand and others not? Reformed (Calvinist) readers see God’s sovereign grace at work: the secret ‘has been given’ to some and not to others. Calvin wrote that the only reason for the distinction is ‘that God calls to himself those whom he has gratuitously elected’, yet he insisted that ‘the blame rests wholly on themselves, because this blindness is voluntary.’ Cooper also stresses that the disciples were chosen. Wesley, giving the Arminian (Wesleyan) reading, put the weight on the hearers’ prior choice: ‘They would not see before now they could not, God having given them up to the blindness which they had chosen’. Some, reported by English and Cooper, take ‘so that’ to describe the result of Jesus’ parables rather than their aim. English’s own conclusion is that parables invite faith but do not enforce it: ‘parables alone will not produce faith, otherwise all who hear would believe’. Calvin, Wesley, English and Cooper each, in their own terms, hold the outsiders responsible for their refusal. See also the note on Matthew 13:10–17.

b: Isaiah 6 is quoted several times in the New Testament: in all three Synoptic Gospels, in John 12:39–41, and by Paul in Rome (Acts 28:25–27). Each time it explains why God’s messengers were not believed.

Paul also speaks of God’s ‘mystery’ now revealed (1 Corinthians 2:7–10) and says the gospel is veiled to those whose minds ‘the god of this age has blinded’ (2 Corinthians 4:3–4), a passage Calvin quotes here.

l.t: Ever hearing, never understanding.
Matthew: blessed are your eyes.
Luke: the mysteries given to you.
Isaiah saw Jesus’ glory.
Paul quotes Isaiah 6 in Rome.
God’s hidden wisdom revealed by the Spirit.
The gospel veiled, and light in our hearts.
Even the disciples: eyes that do not see.

qs: What does Jesus say has been given to his disciples, and what is said about those outside?
How can the same parable open some people’s eyes and leave others blind?
What questions about Jesus would you like to bring to him, as the disciples did?

4.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained
4.ctx: Away from the crowd, Jesus explains the sower to his disciples. Calvin notes that Mark alone includes Jesus’ opening rebuke, and Jesus treats this parable as the key to the rest.
4.mean: Jesus begins with a gentle rebuke: ‘Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables?’ This parable is the key that unlocks the others, because it is about how people hear God’s word. ‘The farmer sows the word.’ The seed is God’s message, the good news of the kingdom that Jesus was preaching (1:14–15). The ESV Study Bible explains that the sower is Jesus first, and then everyone who faithfully passes on his message. The four kinds of ground are four kinds of hearers. The path is the person on whom the word makes no impression at all. Satan snatches it away at once, as birds pick up seed from hard ground. The rocky ground is the person who welcomes the word with joy, but only on the surface. There is no root, and when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, they quickly fall away. The thorny ground is the person who hears and seems to grow, but ‘the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things’ crowd in and choke it. Nothing is ever harvested. The good soil is the person who hears the word, receives it, and produces a crop, some thirtyfold, some sixtyfold, some a hundredfold. Notice that every kind of hearer hears the word. The difference is what happens next. Hearing is not enough; the word must be received, must put down roots, and must be given room to grow. Notice also that not all good soil yields the same. Calvin points out that the thirtyfold is still called good soil; nobody is told to despise those who bear less fruit. Wesley saw a warning for those who have received the word: ‘The desire of any thing, otherwise than as it leads to happiness in God, directly tends to barrenness of soul.’ The parable invites you to examine your own heart, and to let God’s word take root and bear fruit there.
4.big: Jesus explains that the seed is God’s word and the soils are different hearers: only those who receive the word and let it take root bear lasting fruit.

vv.h: Do you not understand this parable? Then how will you understand any of the parables?
b: Calvin noted that in Mark, unlike Matthew and Luke, Jesus indirectly rebukes the disciples for being slow. Wesley called this parable ‘as it were the foundation of all those that I shall speak hereafter’. The ESV Study Bible warns that even disciples can suffer from hard hearts, as Mark will show again (8:17–18).

vv.h: The farmer sows the word
b: Cooper suggests that ‘the word’ can be both the message Jesus preached and Jesus himself, the Word in person. The ESV Study Bible identifies the sower first with Jesus and then with every faithful preacher of the gospel. Calvin stressed that the gospel is ‘always a fruitful seed as to its power, but not as to its produce’: the fault is never in the seed.

vv.h: As soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes away the word
b: Like birds waiting at sowing time, the enemy snatches the word before it can take root. Calvin likened the path to ground trodden hard ‘like a pavement’. Cooper describes such hearers as people who never even think to question their response to the gospel.

vv.h: they themselves have no root, and they remain for only a season
b: Calvin called this ‘temporary faith’: it promises fruit but the heart is not truly changed. Luke says such hearers ‘believe for a season’ (Luke 8:13). Whether such people were ever truly converted is discussed below (Where readings differ).

vv.h: the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things
b: Cooper links the three thorns to anxious unbelief, the self-sufficiency that wealth brings, and the love of this world. Calvin called riches ‘imposing or deceitful’. Wesley commented, ‘A deep and important truth! The desire of any thing, otherwise than as it leads to happiness in God, directly tends to barrenness of soul.’ The rich man of 10:17–22 is an example.

vv.h: They hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold
b: The ESV Study Bible describes the good soil as a consistently attentive and accepting heart. Calvin noted that Christ ‘does not now speak of the perfection of faith’, and that even the thirtyfold soil is called good. Mark’s list rises from thirty to a hundred, the reverse of Matthew’s order (Matthew 13:23).

4.diff: Were the rocky and thorny hearers ever truly converted? Reformed (Calvinist) readers usually see them as people whose faith was never real. Calvin said such hearers ‘are not truly regenerated by the incorruptible seed’ (not truly born again), and that faith the Spirit has once engraved on the heart cannot be destroyed. Cooper writes that the parable does not teach that Christians can lose their salvation; its emphasis is the harvest. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers allow that some may have truly believed for a time, noting Luke’s wording that they ‘believe for a season’ (Luke 8:13). Commenting on Matthew’s version, Wesley said the rocky-ground hearer had ‘No deep work of grace’, but the thorny-ground hearer ‘hath root in himself is deeply convinced, and in a great measure inwardly changed’, and is still choked. On both readings the parable calls every hearer to make sure the word has taken root and is bearing fruit. See also the note on Matthew 13:18–23.

b: Peter writes that believers have been born again ‘not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God’ (1 Peter 1:23), a passage Calvin connects with this parable. James urges his readers to ‘humbly accept the word planted in you’ and to do what it says, not hearers only (James 1:21–22).
Paul warns that the desire to be rich plunges people into ruin (1 Timothy 6:9–10), and Jesus himself will warn how hard it is for the rich to enter God’s kingdom (10:23–25).

l.t: Matthew: hears and understands.
Luke: with a noble and good heart.
Born again of imperishable seed.
Accept the word planted in you; do it.
The rich man and the camel.
Those who want to be rich.
Whoever remains in me bears much fruit.

qs: What happens to the word in each of the four kinds of hearer?
Why are hearing the word and receiving it not the same thing?
Which ‘thorns’ are most likely to crowd out God’s word in your life, and what could you do about them?

4.ctx: Jesus is still speaking about hearing. The ESV Study Bible compares God’s rule and presence to bringing an oil lamp into a room. Matthew and Luke record these sayings too, some of them in other settings (Matthew 5:15; 7:2; 10:26; 13:12); Luke keeps them after the sower, as Mark does (Luke 8:16–18).
4.mean: Jesus asks a question with an obvious answer: ‘Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed?’ Of course not. You light a lamp so that it can be seen and give light to the room. Then he explains that nothing hidden will stay hidden: what is concealed now will be brought into the light. Jesus has just said that the mystery of the kingdom is hidden from those outside (4:11). Now he adds that it will not stay hidden for ever. For now God’s kingdom is veiled in parables and in a teacher from Nazareth; but light is meant to shine. Wesley paraphrased Jesus: ‘I give you this light, not to conceal, but to impart it to others.’ What the disciples hear in private they will one day proclaim openly, and at the end everything will come to light. Then comes a warning about how you hear. ‘Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you, and even more will be added to you.’ Think of a merchant measuring out grain: the size of the scoop you use decides what comes back to you. The ESV Study Bible explains that the measure is the attitude with which you receive Jesus’ word. If you take it in seriously, God gives more understanding and blessing. Then he adds that whoever has will be given more, and whoever does not have will lose even what he has. This sounds unfair at first, but it describes how spiritual life works. Those who welcome God’s word and act on it grow in understanding. Those who neglect it lose even what little they had, like the seed taken from the path. English puts it simply: ‘To hear the message is not a neutral affair.’ Every time you hear God’s word, you are either growing towards the light or drifting away from it.
4.big: God’s light is meant to shine, and what is hidden now will be revealed; so listen carefully, because those who receive the word gain more, and those who neglect it lose what they have.

vv.h: Does anyone bring in a lamp to put it under a basket or under a bed?
b: Cooper reports Augustine Stock’s observation that the Greek reads literally the lamp comes; if so, Jesus may be speaking of himself as the light who has come into the world. The ESV Study Bible compares God’s rule and presence to bringing a lamp into a room: it shows up what was hidden, such as a hard heart or hidden sin. Matthew uses the same saying of the disciples as the light of the world (Matthew 5:14–16).

vv.h: For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed
b: English explains that the mystery of the kingdom, hidden for now, will not remain hidden for ever: God is revealing it in Jesus. Wesley read Jesus as saying that if he hides anything now, ‘it is only that it may be more effectually manifested hereafter.’ Matthew places a similar saying in Jesus’ instructions to the Twelve (Matthew 10:26).

vv.h: Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you use, it will be measured to you
b: Cooper notes that ‘hear’ in the Bible often includes acting on what you hear. Wesley explained: ‘according to the improvement you make of what you have heard, still further assistance shall be given.’ Calvin said that God gives a taste of his teaching ‘on the express condition, that we feed on it abundantly from day to day’. In Matthew the measure saying is about judging others (Matthew 7:2); here it is about receiving God’s word.

vv.h: For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him
b: The ESV Study Bible explains the paradox: whoever welcomes God’s rule receives more of its fruit (4:13–20), while whoever relies on his own resources without receiving the word loses even what he has. Luke has ‘even what he thinks he has’ (Luke 8:18), which Calvin said softens the harshness. Wesley defined ‘he that hath’ as one who ‘improves whatever he has received, to the good of others, as well as of his own soul.’

Jesus calls himself ‘the light of the world’ (John 8:12), and tells his disciples that they are the light of the world too (Matthew 5:14). What he teaches them privately they are to proclaim ‘from the housetops’ (Matthew 10:27).
Paul looks forward to the day when the Lord ‘will bring to light what is hidden in darkness’ (1 Corinthians 4:5).

l.t: Luke: take care how you listen.
Matthew: let your light shine.
Nothing concealed that will not be disclosed.
With the measure you use.
Whoever has will be given more.
I am the light of the world.
What is hidden brought to light.
Doers of the word, not hearers only.

qs: What do the lamp and the measure have to do with hearing?
Why does Jesus say that those who have will be given more?
How could you ‘pay attention’ to God’s word more carefully this week?

4.ctx: This short parable is found only in Mark. It follows the sower and, like it, uses a picture from Galilean farming. The closing words echo Joel 3:13, where the harvest is a picture of God’s judgment.
4.mean: Jesus tells a very simple story. A man scatters seed on his field. Then he goes about his ordinary life: night after night he sleeps, day after day he gets up. Meanwhile, without his help, the seed sprouts and grows, ‘though he knows not how’. The earth produces the crop ‘all by itself’: first the green stalk, then the head of grain, then the full grain ripening in the head. When the grain is ripe, the farmer swings the sickle, ‘because the harvest has come.’ The phrase ‘all by itself’ translates a Greek word that gives us ‘automatic’. The farmer did his part by sowing, and he will do his part at harvest; but the growth itself is not his doing. God gives it. This parable meets a worry the sower might raise. If so much seed is lost on bad ground, will anything come of it? Jesus answers that God’s kingdom is growing, steadily and quietly, even when nobody can see how. Calvin thought Jesus was speaking especially to preachers and teachers, so that they would not lose heart when results were slow, but would sow faithfully and leave the growth to God, like farmers who ‘go to bed and rise again’. Notice too that the growth comes in stages. The ESV Study Bible notes that many in Jesus’ day expected God’s kingdom to arrive suddenly and all at once. Jesus says it begins quietly and grows gradually, through all kinds of opposition, until the harvest. The ESV Study Bible takes the harvest as the last judgment at the end of the age (compare Joel 3:13; Revelation 14:15), while Wesley reads the whole parable of the ‘inward kingdom’ growing in a person. For anyone who shares the good news, this is both a relief and an encouragement. You cannot make faith grow in someone else, any more than a farmer can make wheat grow. You can sow, pray and wait, trusting that God is at work below the surface, and that his harvest will come.
4.big: God’s kingdom grows by God’s own power, quietly and in stages, whether or not people can see how, until the harvest at the end.

vv.h: The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground
b: Wesley read the seed as God’s word, which a preacher sows in the heart, and the kingdom as the ‘inward kingdom’ growing in a person. Calvin applied it to ‘the ministers of the word’. English thought Jesus was encouraging disciples discouraged by the sower: they are not the only ones at work.

vv.h: Night and day he sleeps and wakes, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how
b: Cooper notes that the verbs describe repeated action over a long time. The farmer’s rest is not laziness but trust: he has done his part. Wesley wrote, ‘Even he that sowed it cannot explain how it grows’. Calvin pictured farmers who ‘do not torment themselves with uneasiness and anxiety, but go to bed and rise again’.

vv.h: All by itself the earth produces a crop—first the stalk, then the head, then grain that ripens within
b: ‘All by itself’ is the Greek automatē, from which ‘automatic’ comes. The ESV Study Bible explains it as growth without human effort, and says that ‘first the stalk, then the head’ went against the popular expectation that God’s kingdom would come suddenly and all at once. English adds: ‘Without human assistance there is a power for new life and growth at work’, and links it with Paul’s teaching on the work of the Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:10–12).

vv.h: he swings the sickle, because the harvest has come
b: The words echo Joel 3:13: ‘Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe’ (BSB footnote). In Joel the harvest is God’s judgment on the nations. The ESV Study Bible takes the sickle and harvest here as pictures of the last judgment; Wesley wrote, ‘God cutteth down and gathereth the corn into his garner.’ The kingdom that begins quietly will reach its completion when Jesus returns.

Paul uses the same picture: ‘neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything, but only God, who makes things grow’ (1 Corinthians 3:7). James urges patience like a farmer’s, waiting for the land to yield its crop (James 5:7).
Revelation pictures the end of the age as a harvest: an angel calls, ‘Swing Your sickle and reap’ (Revelation 14:15).

l.t: Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe.
God makes it grow.
The farmer waits patiently.
The harvest of the earth.
The Spirit searches all things.
Another harvest parable: the weeds.

qs: What does the farmer do, and what happens without him?
Why might this parable have encouraged disciples who were discouraged by small results?
Where do you need to trust God for growth you cannot see or control?

4.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
4.ctx: The mustard plant grew in Galilee from a tiny seed into a large shrub. The mustard seed was a byword for something very small (compare Matthew 17:20). Mark then sums up Jesus’ use of parables (4:33–34).
4.mean: Jesus asks how best to picture God’s kingdom, and answers with another seed. A mustard seed is tiny, in Jesus’ words ‘the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth’. Yet once it is planted it grows into ‘the largest of all garden plants’, with branches big enough for birds to nest in its shade. The contrast is the point. Look at what Jesus had in Galilee: a few fishermen, a tax collector, crowds who came and went, leaders plotting against him, and a family who thought he was mad. It hardly looked like the kingdom of God. The ESV Study Bible notes that a small, unnoticed beginning was different from what was popularly expected. Jesus says the kingdom begins as something almost nobody notices, and grows into something great. Calvin wrote that ‘the Lord opens his reign with a feeble and despicable commencement, for the express purpose, that his power may be more fully illustrated by its unexpected progress.’ The picture of birds nesting in the branches echoes Old Testament images of a great kingdom sheltering many peoples (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12). Cooper suggests that the birds may point to the nations who will find shelter in God’s kingdom. The ESV Study Bible sees them as a sign of God’s blessing. Mark then sums up Jesus’ teaching method. Jesus spoke the word in many parables like these, ‘to the extent that they could understand’. He did not overload people; he met them where they were. Wesley called that ‘A rule never to be forgotten by those who instruct others.’ But privately, to his own disciples, he explained everything. The crowd heard enough to make them think. Those who stayed close to Jesus learned more. The same is true now. God’s kingdom often looks small and weak, but it is growing, and the way to understand it is to stay close to the One who explains it.
4.big: God’s kingdom starts as small as a mustard seed but grows into something great that gives shelter to many.

vv.h: a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth
b: Is the mustard seed really the smallest seed? English points out that it ‘was not the smallest seed, but proverbially it seems to have been the typical small seed’ (compare Matthew 17:20; Luke 17:6). The ESV Study Bible calls it ‘the smallest of all the seeds’ and refers to its note on Matthew 13:31–32, which was not read for this note. On English’s reading, Jesus is using the proverbial picture of a tiny seed that his hearers knew.

vv.h: it grows to be the largest of all garden plants and puts forth great branches, so that the birds of the air nest in its shade
b: The ESV Study Bible says the bush could grow ‘as large as 3 by 12 feet (0.9 by 3.7 m)’. English notes that Mark calls it a garden plant and has the birds in its shade, while Matthew and Luke call it a tree with birds in its branches (Matthew 13:32; Luke 13:19); all three stress the contrast in size. Some interpreters, Cooper reports, read the birds negatively, as Satan’s messengers or a sign of the church growing too institutional; Cooper replies that ‘The actual text, however, does not bear out this kind of interpretation’.

vv.h: With many such parables Jesus spoke the word to them, to the extent that they could understand
b: Mark gives a selection, not all of Jesus’ parables (English). Wesley wrote that Jesus was ‘Adapting it to the capacity of his hearers’. The ESV Study Bible notes that the parables also warned his opponents, ‘who might yet turn to him’. Calvin thought Jesus used parables to keep his hearers attentive until the time was right for fuller teaching.

vv.h: He did not tell them anything without using a parable. But privately He explained everything to His own disciples
b: The ESV Study Bible calls this a broad generalization: Jesus regularly included parables in his teaching, not that he spoke only in parables. English notes that ‘explain’ literally means to untie: Jesus untangled the knots for those who stayed with him.

Ezekiel pictures God planting a tender shoot that becomes a majestic cedar: ‘Birds of every kind will nest under it, taking shelter in the shade of its branches’ (Ezekiel 17:23). Nebuchadnezzar’s dream shows a great tree in whose branches ‘the birds of the air nested’ (Daniel 4:12).
Zechariah asks, ‘who has despised the day of small things?’ (Zechariah 4:10). The book of Acts tells how the small band of disciples became a movement reaching Rome (Acts 1:8; 28:30–31).

Why would this parable have mattered to disciples who looked few and weak?
Where might you be tempted to judge God’s work by how small it looks?

4.ctx: It is evening on the day of the parables. The Sea of Galilee lies about 212 metres (696 feet) below sea level, surrounded by hills, and sudden violent storms are common. Several of the disciples were fishermen who knew the lake well.
4.mean: At the end of a long day of teaching, Jesus says, ‘Let us cross to the other side.’ The disciples take him in the boat ‘since He was already in the boat’, and other boats come too. Then a violent windstorm sweeps down on the lake. Waves break over the boat, and it begins to fill with water. These are experienced fishermen, and they are terrified. And Jesus? He is in the stern, asleep on a cushion. He is truly human and truly tired. They wake him with a desperate, accusing question: ‘Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?’ Jesus gets up and rebukes the wind. He commands the sea, ‘Silence!’ and ‘Be still!’ Wesley noted that the word literally means ‘Be thou gagged’; it is the same command Jesus gave to a demon in 1:25. At once the wind dies down, and there is a great calm. Then Jesus turns to the disciples. ‘Why are you so afraid?’ he asks. ‘Do you still have no faith?’ They had been with him, had seen his power, and had just heard him teach about trusting God’s quiet work. Yet in the storm they thought he did not care. English sums up the problem: ‘They needed him to do things: he wanted them to trust him.’ Calvin was careful to add that not every fear is wrong; what Jesus rebukes is fear that pushes out trust. Now the disciples are filled with a different fear, the awe people feel in the presence of God. ‘Who is this,’ they ask, ‘that even the wind and the sea obey Him?’ The Old Testament had the answer. It is the LORD who ‘calmed the storm to a whisper’ (Psalm 107:29) and who rules the raging sea (Psalm 89:9). The man asleep in the stern is the Lord of the sea. Mark wants every reader, in every storm, to ask the disciples’ question and to discover that it is enough to have Jesus in the boat.
4.big: Jesus, tired enough to sleep in a storm, stills the wind and sea with a word, showing that he is the Lord of creation and calling his disciples to trust him.

vv.h: When that evening came ... And there were other boats with Him
b: Calvin noted that Mark alone dates this to the evening of the day of the parables. English sees eyewitness details here: the time, Jesus asleep in the stern, the stark words, and the other boats, which play no further part in the story. Wesley explained ‘since He was already in the boat’: they carried him off in the same boat from which he had been preaching.

vv.h: a violent windstorm came up, and the waves were breaking over the boat
b: The ESV Study Bible explains that the lake lies 696 feet (212 m) below sea level, which causes violent downdrafts and sudden storms (see History). Calvin thought the storm was no accident: it was allowed so that the disciples might discover how weak their faith still was.

vv.h: But Jesus was in the stern, sleeping on the cushion
b: Only Mark mentions the cushion; the ESV Study Bible calls it an eyewitness detail, probably passed on by Peter. Wesley explains it as the place near the rudder. Jesus’ sleep shows his real humanity and fatigue; Calvin rejected the idea that he only pretended to sleep, and said that ‘his divinity watched over him’. Cooper adds that Jesus slept because he trusted his Father. The ESV Study Bible notes a possible echo of Jonah asleep in the storm (Jonah 1:5–6), but Jonah was running from God, while Jesus is bringing people back to God.

vv.h: Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?
b: Mark’s version of their cry is the sharpest; Matthew has ‘Lord, save us!’ and Luke ‘Master, Master, we are perishing!’ (Matthew 8:25; Luke 8:24). Calvin said they were not just praying but expostulating with him, because they ‘attached too much importance to the bodily presence of their Master’. English writes that their question reproaches Jesus for neglecting their safety.

vv.h: Then Jesus got up and rebuked the wind and the sea. “Silence!” He commanded. “Be still!”
b: Jesus speaks to the storm as he spoke to the demon in 1:25. Wesley: ‘Cease thy roaring; literally, Be thou gagged.’ Cooper suggests that this may hint at an evil power behind the storm, though he leaves the question open. English rejects the idea that the words were really addressed to the disciples: Mark ‘clearly believes that Jesus addressed the wind and the waves.’ Calvin noted that the lake had no perception; the command shows that ‘the power of his voice reached the elements’.

vv.h: Do you still have no faith?
b: Jesus first asks, ‘Why are you so afraid?’ Calvin observed that Mark’s ‘so’ shows their fear had gone beyond bounds: ‘It is not every kind of fear that is opposed to faith.’ The ESV Study Bible calls faith, meaning trust in Jesus, the antidote to fear, and notes that the disciples were right to turn to him. Mark will show the disciples struggling to understand again (6:52; 8:17–21).

vv.h: Overwhelmed with fear, they asked one another, “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?”
b: Literally they feared a great fear (Cooper). Their terror of the storm becomes awe at Jesus. The ESV Study Bible calls it the right question, because the calming of the storm shows that ‘this man is also truly God’. The answer to the question runs through the rest of Mark, up to the centurion’s words at the cross (15:39).

hist.t: Storms on the Sea of Galilee
b: The Sea of Galilee is a freshwater lake lying about 212 metres (696 feet) below sea level, ringed by hills. The ESV Study Bible explains that its low position produces violent downdrafts and sudden storms, and Cooper notes that such storms, rising without warning, are common. Mark’s sudden windstorm matches the conditions these sources describe.

b: Psalm 107 describes sailors caught in a storm who ‘cried out to the LORD in their trouble’; ‘He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed’ (Psalm 107:28–29). Other psalms praise God who stills the roaring seas (Psalm 65:7; 89:9). Jesus does what the psalms say God does.

Later Jesus comes to his disciples walking on the water in another storm (6:45–52). The letter to the Hebrews says that through the Son God made the universe and that he sustains all things by his powerful word (Hebrews 1:2–3).

5.ctx: Straight after the storm, Jesus and his disciples land on the east side of the Sea of Galilee, ‘in the region of the Gerasenes’. This was largely Gentile country, part of the area Mark calls the Decapolis (‘Ten Cities’, 5:20). English thinks the crossing was probably a deliberate step into Gentile territory at a time when Jesus was meeting opposition at home.
5.mean:
The boat lands, and at once a man comes out of the tombs to meet Jesus. Mark describes him slowly so that we feel how far gone he is. He lives among the graves and has snapped every chain used to restrain him. Night and day he screams in the hills and cuts himself with stones. Calvin thought the spirit kept him among the tombs so that he would feel cut off from the living, as if he already belonged to the dead.

Yet when he sees Jesus, he runs to him and falls on his knees. Then the spirit cries out through him, ‘What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God? I beg You before God not to torture me!’ Jesus has already ordered it to leave. He asks its name, and the answer is ‘Legion, for we are many.’ A Roman legion was a unit of several thousand soldiers, so the name says the man is occupied by a whole army of evil.

The spirits beg to enter a large herd of pigs on the hillside. Jesus allows it, and about two thousand pigs rush down the bank into the sea and drown. Mark does not say why Jesus allowed it, and the commentators offer different suggestions (see Verse by verse). What is clear is that Jesus is in full command: he decides where the spirits go, and the man is set free.

The local people come and find him ‘sitting there, clothed and in his right mind’. That is the change the story turns on. But they are afraid, and they ask Jesus to leave. English draws the lesson: a great miracle does not by itself produce faith. The freed man, by contrast, begs to go with Jesus. Jesus says no, and sends him home with a task: ‘tell them how much the Lord has done for you’. He goes through the Decapolis telling ‘how much Jesus had done for him’. Mark lets the two phrases stand side by side.
5.big: Jesus frees a man tormented by a ‘legion’ of unclean spirits in Gentile country; the townspeople ask him to leave, but the man he healed becomes his witness.

vv.h: On the other side of the sea, they arrived in the region of the Gerasenes
b: The manuscripts differ on the name: the BSB notes that some read Gadarenes and others Gergesenes, and Matthew has ‘Gadarenes’ (Matthew 8:28). English thinks copyists may have tried to correct a name that seemed to fit the lake badly. See History.

vv.h: He was met by a man with an unclean spirit, who was coming from the tombs
b: Matthew mentions two men (Matthew 8:28). Calvin followed Augustine in thinking there were two, and that Mark and Luke tell of the better-known one; Wesley thought Mark describes the fiercer of the two. The ESV Study Bible sees the spirit’s aim in his isolation, his strength and his self-harm: to destroy a person made in God’s image.

vv.h: He ran and fell on his knees before Him
b: Cooper notes that the word means he worshipped, acknowledging someone greater. Calvin read it as forced homage: the spirits were ‘drawn by a secret exercise of his authority’, so that the whole of Satan’s kingdom is shown to be under Christ. The ESV Study Bible allows that the man himself may also have longed to be free.

vv.h: “What is your name?” ... “My name is Legion,” he replied, “for we are many.”
b: A full-strength Roman legion had about 6,000 soldiers; Calvin and the ESV Study Bible both take the name to mean a great number, not an exact count. English notes that knowing a name was believed to give power over the one named: the spirits shout Jesus’ name and get nowhere, while Jesus asks theirs.

vv.h: The herd of about two thousand rushed down the steep bank into the sea
b: Pigs were unclean under the law of Moses (Leviticus 11:7). Why Jesus allowed their destruction is not explained. Cooper lists several suggestions: the violence of the spirits’ leaving fell on the pigs and not the man; it gave everyone visible proof that the man was free; it showed that the spirits want nothing less than destruction. Calvin thought the spirits meant to turn the people against God through their loss, and that Jesus allowed it to test them; he adds that the reason is not known for certain.

vv.h: Sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid
b: Calvin thought the people’s fear was partly awe at God’s power and partly worry about their losses; ‘the loss of their swine gives them more alarm than the salvation of their soul would give them joy.’ Cooper points out that those tending the pigs were not the owners, but knew how the owners would take the loss.

vv.h: Go home to your own people ... and tell them how much the Lord has done for you
b: Elsewhere Jesus tells those he heals to keep quiet (1:44; 5:43). English, Cooper and the ESV Study Bible each suggest that here, in Gentile country, there was less danger of people mistaking Jesus for a political Messiah. Wesley adds that the man’s witness was needed ‘where Christ did not go in person’. Mark then says the man told what Jesus had done. The ESV Study Bible and Cooper both read the change as showing that Jesus shares God’s nature.

hist.t: Gerasa, Gadara or Gergesa: where did it happen?
b: The manuscripts give three names, and the place is debated. The earliest copies of Mark and Luke read ‘Gerasenes’; Matthew has ‘Gadarenes’ (Matthew 8:28); other copies have ‘Gergesenes’ (BSB footnote). The Lexham Bible Dictionary (S. M. Kraeger) sets out three candidates: Gerasa, the large city at modern Jerash, more than 30 miles from the lake; Gadara, a Greek city about six miles south-east of the lake at modern Umm Qeis; and Gergesa, on the east shore at modern El Koursi (Kursi).

Each has a difficulty. Gerasa fits the earliest text of Mark but is too far away for the herdsmen and townspeople to come and go the same day (5:14–15); Mark may mean the wider region, named after its best-known city. Gadara, Kraeger says, fits the Gentile setting and the short time involved, though English counts it, too, as several miles from the lake. Gergesa fits the geography best, with steep slopes and ancient caves by the shore, but the earliest witness to it is Origen in the third century. He argued that Gerasa ‘has near it neither sea nor lake’, and that a steep place at Gergesa was pointed out as the spot. Kraeger thinks Origen may have had no manuscript behind his suggestion.

English, following Cranfield, and the ESV Study Bible both think Mark meant a small place on the shore, recalled in the name Kursi, and the ESV Study Bible notes a fifth-century church excavated there that ‘possibly marks’ the traditional site. Kraeger notes that there is no archaeological evidence for a second, lakeside Gerasa, and leaves the question open; none of these sources reports a clear majority. Whichever name is original, Mark sets the story across the lake in the Decapolis (5:20), largely Gentile territory.

5.ctx: Jesus is back on the Galilean (Jewish) side of the lake, where crowds gather wherever he goes. Mark sets one story inside another, as he did in 3:20–35: a woman’s healing interrupts the journey to Jairus’s house. English notes that the device places two very different people side by side.
5.mean:
A synagogue leader named Jairus pushes through the crowd and falls at Jesus’ feet. He is a respected man, yet he begs: ‘My little daughter is near death. Please come and place Your hands on her, so that she will be healed and live.’ Jesus goes with him.

On the way someone else reaches him. For twelve years a woman has suffered from bleeding. She has spent everything on doctors and only grown worse. Under the law of Moses a discharge of blood made a woman ritually unclean, and anyone she touched became unclean too (Leviticus 15:19–27). Mark does not mention this, but several commentators think it helps explain why she comes up quietly from behind. She tells herself, ‘If only I touch His garments, I will be healed’, and touches his cloak. At once the bleeding stops, and she can feel that she is healed.

Jesus stops. He knows that power has gone out from him, and he asks, ‘Who touched My garments?’ His disciples think the question absurd in such a crush. But he keeps looking, and the woman comes forward, trembling, and tells him everything. Jesus does not scold her. He calls her ‘Daughter’ and says, ‘your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.’ Calvin thought there may have been ‘a mixture of sin and error’ in her faith, yet Jesus honoured it.

Then comes the news Jairus dreaded: his daughter has died. Jesus says, ‘Do not be afraid; just believe.’ He takes Peter, James and John with him. At the house the mourners are already wailing, and when Jesus says the child is ‘not dead, but asleep’, they laugh at him. Inside, he takes her by the hand and says in Aramaic, ‘Talitha koum!’, ‘Little girl, I say to you, get up!’ She gets up and walks. Jesus tells them to keep it quiet and to give her something to eat.

English sees the theme of both stories as true faith: trusting Jesus himself, whether you are a leader at the end of your strength or an outcast nobody wants to touch.
5.big: On the way to raise a synagogue leader’s dying daughter, Jesus heals an unclean woman who touches his cloak; both learn that trusting him is stronger than fear, illness and death.

vv.h: A synagogue leader named Jairus arrived, and seeing Jesus, he fell at His feet
b: A synagogue leader organised the services. The ESV Study Bible says these were laymen. English notes that, after so much opposition from leaders, here is one who welcomes Jesus. Calvin took the kneeling as respect for ‘a prophet of God’, and judged Jairus’s faith weak, since he thought Jesus had to come and touch the girl; yet Jesus went.

vv.h: A woman was there who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years
b: Leviticus 15:25 says that a woman with such a discharge ‘will be unclean all the days of her unclean discharge’. Mark does not mention uncleanness, so how far it shaped her actions is an inference. English thinks it ‘may account in part’ for her coming from behind; Wesley (on Matthew 9:22) thought she was afraid partly for this reason. The ESV Study Bible goes further, saying her condition barred her from the women’s court of the temple and required her to warn people in public. Cooper thinks that, as an outcast, she could not approach him openly, so she came secretly, and it was enough.

vv.h: At once Jesus was aware that power had gone out from Him
b: Calvin insisted that Jesus healed her ‘knowingly and willingly’: he asked the question so that she would make it known in public. The woman’s ‘fear’ uses a word that can also mean awe, and the ESV Study Bible suggests she may also have feared having made others unclean on her way through the crowd. Cooper suggests that Jesus wanted her to confess her faith openly so that he could restore her to the community.

vv.h: your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction
b: The ESV Study Bible notes that the woman nobody would touch is welcomed as family. The verb for ‘healed’ (Greek sōzō) also means ‘saved’. The ESV Study Bible takes it to mean both bodily and spiritual healing; English notes the double meaning but is more cautious. Calvin drew the parallel: as she was healed by faith, so we receive forgiveness by faith. English points out that what Jesus found lacking in his disciples in the storm (4:40), he praises in her.

vv.h: Do not be afraid; just believe
b: English notes the tense: Jairus has already begun to fear, and Jesus tells him to keep on believing. The BSB footnote gives ‘ignored’ as a possible rendering of ‘overheard’: Jesus may have heard the news and refused to be ruled by it.

vv.h: Peter, James, and John the brother of James
b: The same three see the Transfiguration and Gethsemane (9:2; 14:33).

vv.h: The child is not dead, but asleep
b: Was she really dead? The messengers, the mourners and Luke 8:53 all say she was, and the mourners’ laughter shows they were sure; Calvin saw that as confirming the miracle. English rejects the idea of a coma, since Jesus had not yet seen her. English takes the words to mean that her death was like sleep, because Jesus was about to wake her. The ESV Study Bible likewise holds that she had truly died, her death being sleep from Jesus’ point of view. Wesley (on Matthew 9:24) called it ‘only a temporary suspension of sense and motion, which should rather be termed sleep than death’. Calvin noted that Scripture often calls death sleep, a pointer to resurrection (compare John 11:11–14; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–14).

vv.h: “Talitha koum!” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up!”
b: Mark keeps Jesus’ Aramaic words, which the ESV Study Bible and English take as a mark of eyewitness memory. Touching a dead body made a person unclean (Numbers 19:11); as with the woman, Jesus is not made unclean but makes alive. On the order to keep quiet, Wesley thought Jesus wanted to avoid vainglory, crowds and further anger from his opponents.
Elijah and Elisha each raised a dead child (1 Kings 17:17–24; 2 Kings 4:18–37). Later Peter raises Tabitha with almost the same words, ‘Tabitha, get up!’ (Acts 9:40).
In the Gospels uncleanness does not pass to Jesus; instead his touch makes clean, as with the man with leprosy (Mark 1:40–42).

6.ctx: Jesus returns to Nazareth, the village where he grew up (1:9), with his disciples. Earlier his family had tried to take him home, thinking him out of his mind (3:21). The ESV Study Bible sees this visit as closing the section that began with the choosing of the Twelve (3:13–6:6).
6.mean:
On the Sabbath Jesus teaches in the synagogue of his own village. The people who hear him are astonished. ‘Where did this man get these ideas?’ they ask. ‘What is this wisdom He has been given? And how can He perform such miracles?’ Then their questions turn sour. ‘Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?’ They know his trade, his mother and his family. Surely someone so ordinary cannot be special. ‘And they took offense at Him.’ Calvin saw the irony: they admit his wisdom and his miracles, and then use his humble background as a reason to reject both.

Jesus answers with a saying: ‘Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.’ He takes his place in the line of God’s prophets, who were so often rejected by their own people.

Then Mark says something surprising: Jesus ‘could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them.’ Mark does not mean that unbelief made Jesus powerless; he did still heal some. English explains that Jesus does not throw miracles at people from a distance. He works within a relationship of trust, and where there is open hostility the miracles that are meant to show who he is have no place. And Jesus ‘was amazed at their unbelief’. English notes that the Gospels speak of Jesus being amazed in just one other story, at a Roman officer’s faith (Matthew 8:10; Luke 7:9).

Jesus does not stop. He goes round the villages, teaching. Rejection at home does not end his mission. It sends it outward, and the next scene is the sending of the Twelve.
6.big: In his hometown Jesus is dismissed as just the local carpenter; their unbelief limits what he does there, but he goes on teaching in the villages.

vv.h: Where did this man get these ideas? ... And how can He perform such miracles?
b: Calvin noted that they are forced to admire Jesus and still despise him: ‘it is not mere ignorance that hinders men, but that, of their own accord, they search after grounds of offense’. It thinks Jesus was probably invited to speak after the reading of Scripture, as in Luke 4:16–30. Most commentators, it says, take Luke’s account as the same visit, ‘though this is not certain’; Calvin thought Luke 4 described an earlier visit, making this a second rejection. Cooper notes that Jesus arrived with disciples, like a rabbi with his students, so it was natural for the synagogue to invite him to teach.

vv.h: Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary
b: Mark calls Jesus himself ‘the carpenter’, where Matthew has ‘the carpenter’s son’ (Matthew 13:55). Wesley (on Matthew 13:55) explains the Greek word as one who works ‘either in wood, iron, or stone’ (see History), and had ‘no doubt’ that Jesus worked with Joseph in his youth. English thinks ‘son of Mary’ was a disparaging way to speak of him, though Joseph was probably dead; he suggests Mark may also have kept it as fitting the virgin birth (Matthew 1:18–25; Luke 1:26–38). The ESV Study Bible thinks it may hint at a rumour that Jesus was illegitimate. Mark does not explain it.

vv.h: the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?
b: Who these brothers and sisters were is discussed at 3:31 (Where readings differ), which sets out the three main views and the Catholic and Orthodox teaching. Calvin held here, as there, that ‘brothers’ follows a Hebrew idiom for relatives; Wesley (on Matthew 13:55) took them as cousins, sons of another Mary; English and the ESV Study Bible take them as children of Mary and Joseph. James was later one of the church’s ‘pillars’ in Jerusalem (Galatians 2:9), and the ESV Study Bible identifies Judas with the Jude who wrote the letter of that name (Jude 1).

vv.h: Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor
b: Calvin thought this was probably a general proverb. English notes that in calling himself a prophet Jesus chose the most modest title they might accept, and they did not accept even that. Mark alone adds ‘among his relatives’, which recalls 3:21. The ESV Study Bible sees here a preview of his rejection in Jerusalem.

vv.h: So He could not perform any miracles there ... And He was amazed at their unbelief
b: Calvin: unbelievers ‘bind up the hands of God by their obstinacy; not that God is overcome’, but they do not let him show his power. The ESV Study Bible: Jesus will not force miracles on a hostile audience. On his amazement, Wesley comments that Jesus marvelled ‘As man. As he was God, nothing was strange to him.’ English sees it as one of Mark’s pointers to Jesus’ full humanity.

Nazareth was a small Jewish village on a ridge in Lower Galilee. The Lexham Bible Dictionary gives current estimates of 200–500 people in Jesus’ day, living mainly from farming (olives, vines, wheat and barley). It is not mentioned in the Old Testament or by Josephus, though it lay near a town he fortified, and it appears in no non-Christian source of the Roman period, which fits a place of little note (compare John 1:46). Excavations near the Church of the Annunciation have found cisterns, storage silos and tombs.

About 5 km to the north lay Sepphoris. Josephus says Antipas walled it and ‘made it the metropolis of the country’, and the dictionary, citing Jonathan Reed, says it was built into an impressive city early in Jesus’ lifetime. Wesley explains the word translated ‘carpenter’ (Greek tektōn) as a worker ‘either in wood, iron, or stone’. Whether Joseph and Jesus found work at Sepphoris has been much discussed since the 1920s; it is an inference, and the Gospels never mention the city.

6.ctx: Rejected at Nazareth, Jesus goes round the villages teaching (6:6). Now he sends out the Twelve he had appointed ‘to accompany Him, to be sent out to preach’ (3:14). English notes the shift: in the first chapters Jesus calls his followers; from here he sends them.
6.mean:
Jesus calls the Twelve and sends them out in pairs, giving them authority over unclean spirits. Their travelling kit is almost nothing: a staff and sandals, but no bread, no bag, no money and no spare tunic. They are to accept hospitality in the house that welcomes them and stay there until they move on. Where a place will not welcome them or listen, they are to shake the dust off their feet as they leave, ‘as a testimony against them’.

The instructions say a lot about the mission. It is short and urgent; there is no time to equip for a long journey. The disciples are to depend on God, and on the welcome of the people they come to, for food and shelter. Cooper notes that going in pairs gave the strength of two witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6) and bound the Twelve together. Calvin stresses that these rules belonged to this short, temporary mission and were not a fixed rule for all ministers of the word.

The disciples go and do what Jesus has been doing. They preach that people should repent, as he did (1:15). They drive out many demons and heal many of the sick, anointing them with oil. Their authority is entirely borrowed from him: English points out that they had no power over unclean spirits of their own.

The stakes are high on both sides. To welcome the messengers is to welcome their message; to reject them is a serious matter, and the shaken-off dust is a solemn warning. The ESV Study Bible notes that judgment is left to God.

One detail has become a point of difference between churches: the anointing of the sick with oil in verse 13 (see Where readings differ).
6.big: Jesus sends the Twelve out in pairs with almost nothing, to preach repentance, drive out demons and heal, sharing in his own mission.

vv.h: began to send them out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits
b: What was promised at their choosing (3:14–15) now happens. English notes that pairs were a Jewish custom (compare Luke 7:18–19), and Jesus later sends disciples in twos again (11:1; 14:13). Cooper links it with the law’s demand for two witnesses (Deuteronomy 17:6). Calvin took the number twelve as a sign of the restoration of the Church, as Israel came from twelve patriarchs, and saw the miracles as ‘seals’ of the message they preached.

vv.h: Take nothing but a staff for the journey ... and to wear sandals, but not a second tunic
b: Matthew 10:10 and Luke 9:3 forbid a staff, and Matthew also forbids sandals. Calvin thought Matthew and Luke meant a rod that would be a burden, while Mark meant a walking stick. The ESV Study Bible prefers this reading: Matthew and Luke forbid getting new ones, Mark allows those already owned. English admits ‘we do not know why there is this difference’, but notes that the point is the same in all three: travel light, for the task is urgent. The ESV Study Bible hears an echo of the first Passover, eaten with sandals on and staff in hand, ready to leave (Exodus 12:11).

vv.h: When you enter a house, stay there until you leave that area
b: English and Cooper both read this as a warning not to move house in search of better hospitality, which would bring the message into discredit.

vv.h: Shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them
b: English and the ESV Study Bible both say that Jews returning from Gentile lands shook off the dust (the ESV Study Bible cites later rabbinic sources). To do it to a Jewish town was a vivid warning that rejecting the message is serious. Calvin thought it was probably a custom of the time, ‘a sign of execration’. Paul and Barnabas later do this at Pisidian Antioch (Acts 13:51).

vv.h: They also drove out many demons and healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil
b: English notes that oil is linked with miraculous healing in the New Testament only here and in James 5:14, and that it ‘evidently symbolizes’ the word of healing. Calvin rejected the idea that it was medicine, which would have hidden the miracle, and called it a visible sign of the Spirit’s grace. Wesley, linking it with James 5:14–15, said the healing came by God’s blessing, not the oil itself. The ESV Study Bible adds that oil was commonly used with prayer for healing. On the later practice of anointing the sick, see Where readings differ.

6.diff: Is anointing the sick a sacrament? Mark 6:13 is one of two New Testament passages on anointing the sick with oil; the other is James 5:14–15. The Catholic Church teaches that ‘this sacred anointing of the sick was instituted by Christ our Lord as a true and proper sacrament of the New Testament’, which ‘is alluded to indeed by Mark, but is recommended to the faithful and promulgated by James’ (Catechism 1511, quoting the Council of Trent). It adds that it ‘is not a sacrament for those only who are at the point of death’ (Catechism 1514). The Orthodox Longer Catechism counts ‘Unction with Oil’ as a sacrament, in which God’s grace is invoked on the sick ‘to heal him of spiritual and bodily infirmities’, and traces it to the apostles who ‘anointed with oil many that were sick’ (Mark 6:13) (questions 364–365). The Reformed and Methodist traditions recognise two sacraments, baptism and the Lord’s Supper (Westminster Confession 27.4; Methodist Articles of Religion XVI, which says that ‘extreme unction’ is not to be counted a sacrament of the gospel). Calvin read Mark 6:13 as a sign attached to a temporary gift of healing, ‘a temporary seal of the doctrine of the Gospel’, not a lasting ordinance; Wesley called anointing for healing ‘the great standing means’ of healing in the early Church, and contrasted it with extreme unction as given in his day, ‘only when life is despaired of’. Wesley’s point concerns the practice of his day; the Catechism teaches, as quoted above, that the sacrament is not only for those at the point of death.

6.ctx: News of Jesus, now spread further by the Twelve, reaches Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. Mark uses Herod’s reaction to tell, as a flashback, how John the Baptist had died; he first mentioned John’s arrest at 1:14. English notes that this is the one story in Mark not centred on Jesus, and both he and the ESV Study Bible see it as a shadow falling over Jesus’ own path.
6.mean:
People are trying to make sense of Jesus. Some say he is John the Baptist raised from the dead, some that he is Elijah, others that he is a prophet like those of old. Herod has no doubt: ‘John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!’ Calvin saw a bad conscience at work: Herod readily believed what he dreaded.

Mark then goes back to tell what Herod had done. Herod had married Herodias, the wife of his brother (Mark calls him Philip; see History), and John had kept telling him, ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!’ (6:18; compare Leviticus 18:16). So Herod had John arrested. Herodias held a grudge and wanted him dead, but Herod would not allow it. He feared John, ‘knowing that he was a righteous and holy man’, protected him, and liked to listen to him, though what John said left him deeply perplexed. Calvin and English both picture a man pulled two ways: drawn to the truth, but unwilling to give up what John condemned.

Herodias’s chance comes at Herod’s birthday banquet, in front of the leading men of Galilee. Her daughter dances and pleases Herod and his guests, and Herod makes an extravagant promise, sealed with an oath: ‘Whatever you ask of me, I will give you, up to half my kingdom!’ Prompted by her mother, the girl asks for John’s head. Herod is ‘consumed with sorrow’, but ‘because of his oaths and his guests’ he will not refuse. John is beheaded in prison, and his disciples bury him.

The story shows what it can cost to speak God’s truth to the powerful. John loses his life for it, while Herod, though he respects John, cares more about saving face before his guests. English sees John here as a pattern for discipleship, and the ESV Study Bible calls his death an ominous shadow over Jesus’ future. Later another ruler, Pilate, will give way to the crowd and hand Jesus over (15:15), and Jesus’ body too will be laid in a tomb by those who loved him.
6.big: Herod, fearing that Jesus is John raised from the dead, recalls how he had John beheaded to keep a rash oath; John’s faithful death foreshadows Jesus’ own.

vv.h: Now King Herod heard about this, for Jesus’ name had become well known
b: This Herod is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great. Strictly he was a tetrarch, not a king, and Matthew and Luke call him ‘tetrarch’ (Matthew 14:1; Luke 9:7). English suggests Mark’s ‘king’ is an honorary or popular title; Cooper and the ESV Study Bible say the same. The Lexham Bible Dictionary calls Mark’s word incorrect. (See History.)

vv.h: John the Baptist has risen from the dead! ... “He is Elijah,” ... “He is a prophet, like one of the prophets of old.”
b: The same three answers come back when Jesus asks his disciples who people say he is (8:27–28). Elijah was expected to return (Malachi 4:5). Jesus himself later links John with Elijah (9:11–13). The ‘prophet’ may recall the promise of a prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), as the ESV Study Bible and Cooper suggest. Peter’s answer will go beyond all three (8:29).

vv.h: It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!
b: The law forbade a man to marry his brother’s wife while the brother lived (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). Cooper notes that the exception for a brother who died childless did not apply, since Herodias’s first husband was alive. The tense suggests John said it repeatedly (English). Calvin admired John for rebuking the ruler to his face when no one else would: God’s servants need courage when dealing with the powerful.

vv.h: Herod feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man
b: Matthew says Herod himself wanted to kill John but feared the people (Matthew 14:5). Calvin and English both reconcile the two: Herod respected John, but was drawn by Herodias and feared trouble. Wesley comments sharply on ‘he listened to him gladly’: ‘Delusive joy! While Herodias lay in his bosom.’

vv.h: On Herod’s birthday, her opportunity arose
b: The guests are the leading men of government, army and society in Galilee (ESV Study Bible; Wesley). The offer of ‘up to half my kingdom’ echoes the Persian king’s words to Esther (Esther 5:3). Wesley calls it ‘a proverbial expression’, and the ESV Study Bible a figure of speech, not a literal promise. Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome; Mark does not name her.

vv.h: The head of John the Baptist
b: Calvin thought Herodias acted less from revenge than from fear of being cast off: while John lived and spoke, her marriage was under threat. English notes the echo of Jezebel’s hatred of Elijah (1 Kings 16:29–34; 19:1–3), while warning that this need not mean the story was shaped by it.

vv.h: The king was consumed with sorrow, but because of his oaths and his guests, he did not want to refuse her
b: Calvin was blunt: if there had been no witnesses Herod would not have kept his oath; by keeping a foolish promise ‘he committed a more heinous offense’ than by breaking it. Cooper, citing Hendriksen, notes that Herod could have said that he had promised a gift, not a crime. Wesley sets Herod’s ‘honour’ beside the chief priests’ scruple over Judas’s silver (Matthew 27:6): innocent blood troubled neither.

vv.h: They came and took his body and placed it in a tomb
b: Matthew adds that John’s disciples went and told Jesus (Matthew 14:12). Calvin saw in the burial a token of the resurrection, and the disciples’ love at some risk to themselves.

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The Herod of this passage is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, which he ruled for 43 years. Josephus confirms the outline of Mark’s account: Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of Aretas, king of Arabia, to marry Herodias, who had been the wife of his half-brother. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says some Jews thought ‘the destruction of Herod’s army came from God’ as punishment for his killing John, ‘a good man’ who urged the Jews to righteousness and piety. Josephus adds that John was held and put to death at the fortress of Machaerus, which overlooks the Dead Sea from the east.

Josephus gives a political motive: Herod feared that John’s influence over the people might lead to a revolt. The Gospels tell the personal story behind the arrest. Calvin thought the political reason may have been the excuse Herod gave; the two accounts can stand together.

Mark’s ‘king’ is not Antipas’s official title, and Josephus tells how it led to his downfall. In AD 39 Herodias, envious that her brother Agrippa had been made king, urged Antipas to go to Rome and seek the same rank. Agrippa accused him before the emperor Gaius, who took away his territory and banished him to Lyons in Gaul. Herodias went into exile with him.

6.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
6.ctx: The Twelve return from their mission (6:7–13) and report to Jesus. The crowds are so great that they have no time even to eat, so Jesus takes them by boat to a quiet place to rest.
6.mean:
The apostles come back full of news, and Jesus invites them to come away and rest. But the crowd sees where the boat is heading and gets there first on foot. When Jesus steps ashore he does not send them away. ‘He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. And He began to teach them many things.’ The ESV Study Bible hears in the phrase Moses’ prayer for a leader for Israel (Numbers 27:17), and Ezekiel had promised that God would one day shepherd his people himself (Ezekiel 34). Jesus feeds them first with his word.

As evening comes, the disciples urge him to send the people off to buy food. Jesus replies, ‘You give them something to eat.’ They object that it would cost two hundred denarii, about two hundred days’ wages. He tells them to see what they have: five loaves and two fish. He has the people sit down in groups on the green grass, in hundreds and fifties. Then he takes the loaves and fish, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks the loaves and gives them to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is satisfied, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. Five thousand men had eaten.

Scripture echoes run all through the scene. Like Israel fed with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16), the people are fed in a desolate place; the ESV Study Bible concludes that Jesus ‘acts as God acts’. Like the prophet Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty loaves and had some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44), Jesus feeds a multitude, but on a far greater scale. Some readers also hear a forward echo: at the Last Supper Jesus will again take bread, bless it, break it and give it (14:22). English and Cooper both see a link; the ESV Study Bible stresses the manna and does not mention the Supper, and Calvin reads the blessing simply as thanksgiving (see Verse by verse).

The disciples are part of the miracle. Calvin noted that the bread passed through their hands, so that they became servants of Christ’s power. Yet, as Mark will say after the next scene, they did not yet understand what it meant (6:52).
6.big: Moved with compassion for a leaderless crowd, Jesus teaches them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, through the hands of his disciples.

vv.h: Come with Me privately to a solitary place, and let us rest for a while
b: English notes that this is the only certain use of ‘apostles’ in Mark: he thinks the word probably does not belong in the text at 3:14, where the BSB has it. English explains the background as the Jewish idea of an authorised messenger, whose role depends on the one who sends him and ends with the task: function, not status. English and Cooper both note that Jesus cares for the disciples’ tiredness: they need rest, and their later sharp reply (6:37) may show the strain.

vv.h: He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd
b: English explains ‘had compassion’ as being moved inwardly so as to act; in the Gospels the verb is used only of Jesus or of characters in his parables who reflect him, such as the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:33). The ESV Study Bible links ‘sheep without a shepherd’ with Numbers 27:17 and Ezekiel 34, where God promises to shepherd his people himself because their leaders have failed. Calvin noted that, though worn out, Jesus ‘did not spare himself’.

vv.h: You give them something to eat
b: English reads the command as an invitation to share Jesus’ power; their reply shows how little they yet trusted him. Cooper thinks it startled them. The ESV Study Bible calls their answer ‘mild sarcasm’ and notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer (so too the BSB footnote).

vv.h: They sat down in groups of hundreds and fifties
b: John says the loaves were barley loaves (John 6:9), and Cooper notes these were small, cheap loaves eaten by the poor. The ESV Study Bible hears Psalm 23 in the green grass (‘He makes me lie down in green pastures’) and Moses’ organising of Israel into hundreds and fifties (Exodus 18:25). English thinks the groups simply made the meal orderly, and rejects theories that the rows were military ranks. Calvin saw a practical purpose: the crowd could be counted and the miracle witnessed.

vv.h: Looking up to heaven, Jesus spoke a blessing and broke the loaves
b: English notes that taking bread, blessing God and breaking it was what a Jewish father did at any meal. Calvin says ‘blessing’ here means thanksgiving, and that looking up shows earnest prayer; the ESV Study Bible sees Jesus’ dependence on his Father. The same four actions (took, blessed, broke, gave) recur at the Last Supper (14:22). English allows that the account could be described in terms related to the Supper, though he says this need not mean Mark wrote the story because of it. Cooper says the scene prefigured the day when Jesus himself would be ‘the bread that is offered up and broken’. Calvin does not draw the connection here.

vv.h: They all ate and were satisfied
b: Some modern readers suggest the crowd were moved to share hidden food, or that each received only a token morsel. English rejects both: the hunger was real, ‘satisfied’ means a real meal, and the detail points to a miracle. The leftovers recall Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17:16; 2 Kings 4:42–44), as the ESV Study Bible notes. Matthew adds that women and children were also fed (Matthew 14:21).

God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and the psalmist pictures the Lord as a shepherd who leads his flock to green pastures (Psalm 23). Ezekiel promised one shepherd, God’s servant David, who would feed the flock (Ezekiel 34:23).

In John’s account the crowd want to make Jesus king, and the next day he calls himself ‘the bread of life’ (John 6:15, 35). Jesus feeds a second crowd of four thousand in Mark 8:1–10, and later warns the disciples not to forget the baskets of leftovers (8:17–21).

6.ctx: Straight after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and dismisses the crowd. John adds that the people wanted to make him king by force (John 6:15). This is the second time the disciples face a storm on the lake (compare 4:35–41), but this time Jesus is not in the boat with them.
6.mean: Jesus makes the disciples set off across the lake while he sends the crowd home, and then he goes up the mountain to pray. By evening the boat is out in the middle of the sea and Jesus is alone on land. He can see them straining at the oars against a headwind. Between three and six in the morning he comes to them, walking on the sea. Mark adds a puzzling detail: ‘He intended to pass by them.’ Commentators read it differently (see Verse by verse). The ESV Study Bible and Cooper connect the words with the Old Testament, where God ‘passes by’ Moses to reveal his glory (Exodus 33:22; 34:6). Job says that God ‘treads on the waves of the sea’ and that when he passes by, Job cannot see him (Job 9:8, 11). On this reading Jesus is revealing who he is, doing what the Old Testament says God does. The disciples see a figure on the water and cry out, thinking it is a ghost. Jesus speaks at once: ‘Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.’ The words ‘It is I’ (Greek egō eimi) can also be translated ‘I am’. The ESV Study Bible and English both hear an echo of God’s name revealed to Moses, ‘I AM’ (Exodus 3:14); Calvin and Cooper do not comment on an echo, and dwell on the comfort of his presence. Then Jesus climbs into the boat and the wind dies down. Mark ends on a sobering note. The disciples are utterly astounded, ‘for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.’ English explains that each miracle should have shown them that Jesus has the power they would expect of the God of their Scriptures, the God who feeds his people and makes a way through the sea. They had just seen him feed five thousand, and still they did not see who he was. Calvin draws the lesson: we too need the Lord to give us new eyes.
6.big: After feeding the crowd, Jesus prays alone, then comes to his struggling disciples walking on the sea and says ‘It is I’; but their hearts are still hardened.

vv.h: Jesus made His disciples get into the boat and go on ahead of Him to Bethsaida
b: Calvin notes the force of ‘made’: the disciples would not have left him of their own accord; Wesley agrees that they did not care to go without him. Cooper suggests Jesus also wanted to keep them away from the crowd’s plan to make him king (John 6:15). Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida (Luke 9:10), yet here they sail towards it; English notes that Mark is not much concerned with exact places. Jesus then goes to pray. Calvin saw Jesus showing both his natures: as man he prays, though all things are in his power.

vv.h: About the fourth watch of the night, Jesus went out to them, walking on the sea
b: The fourth watch ran from about 3 to 6 a.m. (ESV Study Bible). They had been rowing for hours. Wesley comments that ‘the darkness could veil nothing from him’. The ESV Study Bible notes the lake lies 212 metres (696 feet) below sea level, which makes sudden strong winds common there. It also points to Job 9:8, where God treads on the waves, and Psalm 77; English adds Isaiah 43:16, where God makes a way in the sea.

vv.h: He intended to pass by them
b: The commentators take this in different ways. The ESV Study Bible says Jesus meant them to see him ‘pass by’, as God passed by Moses (Exodus 33:19, 22; 34:6, where the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb) and as Job speaks of God passing by (Job 9:11): an implicit claim to divinity. Cooper reads it the same way, as a reassurance. English is less sure. He sets out three readings: Jesus meant to reach the other side first (which he finds contrived); Jesus acted as if passing by to draw them into deeper understanding, as on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:28), which he finds ‘more convincing’; or Jesus really meant to pass by, to test whether they trusted him. Wesley takes it plainly: Jesus walked as if passing by.

vv.h: Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid
b: English sees the words as recalling God’s own self-revelation (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 41:4; 43:10), but says Jesus does not force on them the faith he seeks. The ESV Study Bible likewise hears an echo of Exodus 3:14. Calvin focuses on the comfort: confidence rests on knowing he is present.

vv.h: For they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened
b: Matthew includes Peter walking on the water and ends with the disciples worshipping Jesus as the Son of God (Matthew 14:28–33); Mark, often linked with Peter, leaves Peter’s part out, which Cooper suggests may be so that the focus stays on the Lord. Wesley insists that ‘hardened’ does not mean the disciples were rejected by God: they were slow and dull of understanding. Calvin calls the loaves ‘a sufficiently bright mirror’ of Christ’s divinity, and says Mark adds their blindness as a warning about our own. The ESV Study Bible: in the earlier storm they struggled with fear; now with fear and hardness of heart as well.

In the Old Testament, walking on the sea and making a way through it belong to God (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19; Isaiah 43:16), and God promises to be with his people when they pass through the waters (Isaiah 43:2). When God passed by Moses he proclaimed his name and character (Exodus 34:6).
The disciples’ hardness continues: when Jesus feeds four thousand they again fail to understand (Mark 8:14–21). John records Jesus’ words on the same night, ‘It is I; do not be afraid’ (John 6:20).

l.t: Peter walks on the water.
‘It is I; do not be afraid’.
He treads on the waves of the sea.
When my glory passes by.
I AM WHO I AM.
When you pass through the waters.
The first storm.
Do you still not understand?

qs: Where was Jesus while the disciples were struggling, and what could he see?
What do you make of Mark’s comment that Jesus ‘intended to pass by them’?
What would it mean for you to hear Jesus say ‘Take courage! It is I’ in a struggle you face now?
