6.ctx: After the night on the lake the boat lands, not at Bethsaida where they were heading (6:45), but at Gennesaret on the western shore. Mark closes this stretch of his Gospel with a summary of Jesus’ healing work, as he did earlier (1:32–34; 3:7–12).
6.mean:
As soon as the boat is moored, people recognise Jesus. Word spreads through the whole region, and they carry the sick on mats to wherever they hear he is. In villages, towns and countryside, they lay the sick in the marketplaces and beg simply to touch the fringe of his cloak. ‘And all who touched Him were healed.’

The scene shows how far Jesus’ fame has spread, and how great his power and compassion are. Everyone who touches him is healed. Yet the commentators also notice what is missing. English points out that Mark mentions no teaching here: people come for healing, and, it seems, for little more. Calvin thought their idea that a touch of his robe was what was needed was partly superstition, but that Jesus graciously met them where they were, so as not to quench a faint and smoking faith (Isaiah 42:3). For us, he adds, we come to Christ now not with hands or eyes but by faith.

English explains the ‘fringe’ of his cloak as the tassels that Jewish men were required to wear on the corners of their garments, as a reminder of God’s commands (Numbers 15:38–39; Deuteronomy 22:12). The woman who touched his cloak in 5:27 had been healed in the same way, and Mark now shows many others doing what she did.

The summary prepares for what follows. In the next chapter the religious leaders come from Jerusalem to question Jesus about purity and tradition (7:1–23). The crowds welcome his healing; the authorities are about to oppose him.
6.big: Wherever Jesus goes in the region of Gennesaret, the sick are brought to him, and all who touch even the fringe of his cloak are healed.

vv.h: When they had crossed over, they landed at Gennesaret and moored the boat
b: English says Gennesaret was ‘probably’ the fertile plain south of Capernaum. They had been heading for Bethsaida (6:45). English says they are generally thought to have been blown off course, and the ESV Study Bible suggests a north-easterly wind drove them south-west. Calvin did not think the exact origin of the name mattered.

vv.h: The people recognized Jesus and ran through that whole region, carrying the sick on mats
b: Cooper notes that Jesus could now go nowhere without being recognised; news of earlier healings had gone ahead of him. The ESV Study Bible observes that by now Jesus is well known throughout Galilee.

vv.h: They ... begged Him just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed
b: English notes that Jewish men were required to wear tassels (Numbers 15:37–41; Deuteronomy 22:12), and that the sense of God’s power in Jesus was so strong that people took touching his clothes to be a way of healing (compare 5:28). The ESV Study Bible likewise speaks of God’s healing power as strongly present. Calvin saw superstition in limiting his grace to a touch of his robe, which Jesus nevertheless bore with; he warned against seeking grace from relics, ‘in wood, or nails, or robes’. Later the apostles’ shadows and handkerchiefs are linked with healing in the same way (Acts 5:15; 19:12).
The tassels on an Israelite’s garment were to remind the wearer of ‘all the commandments of the LORD’ (Numbers 15:39).
Isaiah’s servant would not snuff out a smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3), and Matthew applies the words to Jesus’ healing ministry (Matthew 12:15–21).

l.t: Matthew’s summary.
Tassels on their garments.
A smouldering wick he will not snuff out.
Crowds pressing to touch him.
The woman who touched his cloak.
The sick laid in the streets.

qs: What did the people of Gennesaret do when they recognised Jesus?
What do you think was right, and what was missing, in the crowd’s eagerness to touch him?
How do we come to Jesus for help today, when we cannot touch his cloak?

7.ctx: The ‘tradition of the elders’ was an oral body of rules that Pharisees believed went back to Moses, later written down in the Mishnah. Hand-washing before meals was a ritual purity custom extended from priests to everyone, not a matter of hygiene. ‘Corban’ meant a gift dedicated to God.
7.mean: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem see Jesus’ disciples eating with unwashed hands and ask why they ignore the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers with Isaiah 29:13: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.’ ‘You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.’ His example: God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother’, but their rules let a son declare his money ‘Corban’, devoted to God, and so refuse to support his parents. ‘Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down.’
7.big: Religious rules can become a way of avoiding what God actually commands.
7.diff: Scripture and tradition. Protestants read this passage as a warning that all church traditions must be tested by Scripture, the only infallible rule (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10). Calvin drew the principle that ‘all kinds of worship invented by men are of no estimation in his sight’. Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree that merely human traditions can contradict God’s word, but distinguish them from apostolic Tradition, which hands on what the apostles received and which they hold together with Scripture as one deposit of revelation. The Catholic Catechism distinguishes that Tradition from ‘the various theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions, born in the local churches over time’ (80–83). All agree that no tradition may be used to cancel a plain command of God, as the Corban rule did.

7.ctx: The food laws of Leviticus 11 marked Israel out from the nations. Whether Gentile Christians had to keep them became a burning issue in the early church (Acts 10; 15; Romans 14).
7.mean: Jesus calls the crowd: ‘Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.’ Food goes into the stomach, not the heart. Mark adds his own comment: ‘(Thus all foods are clean.)’ What defiles is what comes out of the heart: ‘evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness.’
7.big: Our real problem is not outside us but inside; and Christ’s coming ends the food laws that once marked Israel off.
7.diff: Almost all churches read Mark’s comment as declaring the Old Testament food laws fulfilled and no longer binding (compare Acts 10:15; Romans 14:14). Seventh-day Adventists hold that the distinction between clean and unclean meats still applies as a matter of health. The BSB footnote gives an alternative translation of verse 19 that applies the words to digestion, but most translations follow the reading in the text.

src.l: Seventh-day Adventist Church, 28 Fundamental Beliefs, no. 22 ‘Christian Behavior’

7.h: The Faith of the Gentile Woman
7.ctx: Tyre was a wealthy Gentile city on the coast, north-west of Galilee. Jews sometimes called Gentiles ‘dogs’; the word Jesus uses here can mean little dogs or house dogs (BSB footnote: ‘puppies’).
7.mean: Jesus goes into Gentile territory and tries to stay hidden. A Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin falls at his feet and begs him to free her daughter from a demon. ‘First let the children have their fill,’ he says. ‘For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.’ Israel comes first in God’s plan. She does not argue but takes his words and turns them: ‘Yes, Lord,’ ‘even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.’ ‘Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.’ She goes home and finds it so.
7.big: God’s blessing came to Israel first, but a Gentile mother’s humble, persistent faith shows it was always meant for the nations too.

7.ctx: The Decapolis, south-east of the lake, was again Gentile territory. Mark keeps Jesus’ Aramaic word, as at 5:41.
7.mean: People bring a deaf man who can hardly speak. Jesus takes him aside, puts his fingers in his ears, spits and touches his tongue, using touch to communicate with a man who cannot hear. He looks up to heaven, sighs, and says ‘Ephphatha!’ (‘Be opened!’). The man hears and speaks plainly. The crowd say, ‘He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!’, echoing Isaiah 35:5–6, the promise of what God would do when he came to save.
7.big: Jesus does the works Isaiah said would mark God’s coming, and he deals with each person in a way they can understand.

8.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
8.ctx: This second feeding takes place in the largely Gentile region of the Decapolis (7:31). Dalmanutha (verse 10) is otherwise unknown; it was somewhere on the western shore.
8.mean: Another large crowd has been with Jesus three days with nothing to eat. ‘I have compassion for this crowd’, he says. The disciples ask, ‘Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?’, as though the first feeding had never happened. With seven loaves and a few fish he feeds about four thousand, and seven basketfuls are left.
8.big: Jesus’ compassion and provision reach Gentiles as well as Jews.
8.diff: Some scholars think the two feedings are two versions of one event. Mark clearly regards them as two (8:19–20), with different numbers, places and words for ‘basket’. Many see significance in the settings: twelve baskets among Jews, seven among Gentiles.

8.ctx: A ‘sign from heaven’ meant some spectacular proof directly from God, beyond the healings they had already seen.
8.mean: Pharisees come and demand ‘a sign from heaven’, to test him. ‘Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”’ He leaves them.
8.big: Jesus does not perform on demand for people who have already decided not to believe.

8.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod
8.ctx: Leaven (yeast) works its way invisibly through a whole batch of dough; it was a common picture of a spreading corrupt influence.
8.mean: In the boat with one loaf, Jesus warns, ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.’ The disciples think he is talking about bread. He asks a string of searching questions: ‘Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts?’ He reminds them of the twelve and the seven baskets. ‘Do you still not understand?’
8.big: Unbelief can be catching; and even disciples can be slow to see what is in front of them.

8.ctx: This healing, found only in Mark, comes right after Jesus rebukes the disciples for having eyes and not seeing (8:18).
8.mean: At Bethsaida Jesus leads a blind man out of the village, spits on his eyes, lays hands on him and asks, ‘Can you see anything?’ ‘I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.’ Jesus lays hands on him again, ‘and he could see everything clearly.’
8.big: A two-stage healing, placed where Mark puts it, pictures the disciples: they see something of Jesus, but not yet clearly.
8.diff: Some ask whether the first touch ‘failed’. The Gospel does not suggest Jesus was struggling. Most commentators see an acted parable: in the next scene Peter sees that Jesus is the Christ, but blurrily, because he cannot accept a suffering Christ.

b: Bethsaida (‘house of fishing’) was the home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Josephus says that Philip the tetrarch, another son of Herod the Great, enlarged the village and renamed it Julias, in honour of the emperor Augustus’s daughter.

Two sites near the north shore of the lake are proposed. Et-Tell, about 2.5 km inland, has been excavated continuously since 1987 by Rami Arav and Richard Freund. It has impressive Iron Age remains (Arav suggests it was the capital of the Old Testament kingdom of Geshur, 2 Samuel 15:8) and a Roman-period settlement, including a building some excavators identify as a small Roman temple. Critics such as Jodi Magness say its Roman remains are too modest for the town Josephus describes. El-Araj, on the shore, was long thought to have only later remains, but excavations led by Steven Notley and Mordechai Aviam since 2016 have reported a Roman-era bathhouse (1st–3rd centuries AD) and a later Byzantine church. Arav replies that there is not yet evidence of an earlier Jewish fishing village there. Scholars are divided.

8.ctx: This is the turning point of Mark. Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, 40 km north of the lake, a city full of pagan worship.
8.mean: On the road Jesus asks, ‘Who do people say I am?’ They report the popular views: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. ‘But what about you?’ Jesus asked. ‘Who do you say I am?’ Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ.’ Jesus warns them not to tell anyone, because the word ‘Christ’ (Messiah) meant to most people a conquering king, and he must first teach them what kind of Christ he is.
8.big: Everything turns on the question every reader must answer: ‘Who do you say I am?’
8.diff: Peter and the ‘rock’. Mark, traditionally Peter’s Gospel, records only Peter’s confession. Matthew adds Jesus’ reply, ‘on this rock I will build My church’ and the keys (Matthew 16:18–19). Catholic teaching holds that the Church is ‘built on Peter’, who received ‘a unique mission’ that continues in his successors, the bishops of Rome (Catechism 552–553). Orthodox tradition honours Peter’s primacy among the apostles but does not accept the papacy’s claims of jurisdiction. Most Protestants follow Calvin in taking the rock to be Peter as confessor of Christ, or the faith he confessed, which is ‘the common foundation of the whole Church’. See the note on Matthew 16.

hist.t: Caesarea Philippi and the shrine of Pan
b: The city stood beside a large cave from which one of the sources of the Jordan flowed. In the Greek period the cave became a shrine to the god Pan, and the place was called Panias (the modern name is still Banias). About 20 BC the emperor Augustus gave the area to Herod the Great, who built a white marble temple to Augustus there, according to Josephus. Herod’s son Philip developed the town into a city and named it Caesarea in honour of the emperor, adding his own name to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast.
The cave can still be seen at Banias. Many preachers draw out the setting: among shrines to Pan and to a deified emperor, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ.

8.ctx: Nothing in popular Jewish expectation prepared people for a Messiah who would be killed. This is the first of three predictions (compare 9:31; 10:33–34).
8.mean: Now Jesus begins ‘to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again.’ ‘Must’: this is God’s plan, foretold in Scripture. He says it plainly. Peter takes him aside and rebukes him. Jesus, looking at the disciples, rebukes Peter publicly: ‘Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men.’ Moments after confessing Christ rightly, Peter speaks for Satan, offering the same temptation as the wilderness: glory without the cross.
8.big: The Christ must suffer, die and rise; any version of him without the cross is the devil’s idea.

8.ctx: Mark’s first readers knew exactly what ‘take up his cross’ meant: the condemned man carried his own crossbeam to his execution. Some of them may have watched fellow believers die under Nero.
8.mean: Jesus calls the crowd as well as the disciples: ‘If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.’ The logic is the gospel’s paradox: ‘whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.’ ‘What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?’ And whoever is ashamed of Jesus now, ‘the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father’s glory with the holy angels.’
8.big: Following a crucified Messiah means dying to self; but that is the only way to find life.

9.ctx: Moses represented the Law and Elijah the Prophets; both had met God on a mountain (Exodus 24; 1 Kings 19). The cloud recalls God’s glory filling the tabernacle. The mountain is not named.
9.mean: ‘Truly I tell you, there are some standing here who will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrive with power.’ Six days later Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a high mountain, ‘There He was transfigured before them.’ His clothes become ‘radiantly white, brighter than any launderer on earth could bleach them.’ Elijah and Moses talk with him. Peter, terrified, suggests building three shelters, as if the three were equals. A cloud covers them and a voice says: ‘This is My beloved Son. Listen to Him!’ Suddenly they see only Jesus. Coming down, he tells them to tell no one ‘until the Son of Man had risen from the dead.’ They ask about Elijah coming first; Jesus says Elijah has come, and ‘they have done to him whatever they wished’, meaning John the Baptist.
9.big: For a moment the disciples see the glory hidden in Jesus, and the Father tells them to listen to him, above Moses and Elijah.
9.diff: ‘Some standing here’ (verse 1). This saying puzzles readers, since the disciples died before Jesus returned. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, take it to refer to the Transfiguration that immediately follows, a preview of his glory (compare 2 Peter 1:16–18). Calvin took it as the ‘manifestation of heavenly glory, which Christ began to make at his resurrection, and which he afterwards made more fully by sending the Holy Spirit’. Others think of the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Each view finds a real coming of the kingdom ‘with power’ in the disciples’ lifetime.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 8:30–9:1 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Transfiguration’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

9.h: The Boy with an Evil Spirit
9.ctx: While the three were on the mountain, the other disciples had failed to help a desperate father.
9.mean: Jesus comes down to an argument. A father explains that a spirit throws his son down, makes him foam, grind his teeth and become rigid, and has often thrown him into fire and water; the disciples could not drive it out. ‘O unbelieving generation!’ Jesus says. The father pleads, ‘if You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.’ ‘“If You can?” echoed Jesus. “All things are possible to him who believes!”’ ‘Immediately the boy’s father cried out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!”’ Jesus commands the spirit out, and lifts the boy, who looks dead, to his feet. Privately the disciples ask why they failed. ‘This kind cannot come out, except by prayer.’
9.big: Jesus welcomes weak, mixed faith that turns to him; and his followers’ power depends on dependence on God in prayer.
9.diff: ‘Prayer and fasting’. Later manuscripts add ‘and fasting’ in verse 29 (BSB footnote, as in the KJV). The earliest manuscripts have ‘prayer’ only. Epilepsy? The symptoms resemble epilepsy, and Matthew uses a word often translated ‘epileptic’ (17:15). The Gospels present this case as demonic; they do not imply that epilepsy in general is.

9.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion
9.ctx: Jesus is now travelling quietly through Galilee towards Jerusalem.
9.mean: Jesus avoids the crowds ‘because He was teaching His disciples’: ‘The Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men. They will kill Him, and after three days He will rise.’ ‘But they did not understand this statement, and they were afraid to ask Him about it.’
9.big: Jesus kept telling them plainly; they did not want to hear.

9.ctx: In the ancient world children had no status. To welcome a child brought no honour or advantage.
9.mean: In Capernaum Jesus asks what they were arguing about on the road. Embarrassed silence: they had been arguing ‘about which of them was the greatest’, straight after he had spoken of his death. He sits down, as a teacher did, and says, ‘If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all.’ He takes a child in his arms: ‘Whoever welcomes one of these little children in My name welcomes Me’, and the Father who sent him. John reports that they tried to stop someone casting out demons in Jesus’ name ‘because he does not accompany us.’ ‘Do not stop him’, says Jesus. ‘For whoever is not against us is for us.’ Even ‘a cup of water’ given because they belong to Christ will be rewarded.
9.big: Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom is measured by service to the least important; and his people should not be jealous of others working in his name.

9.ctx: ‘Hell’ here is Gehenna (BSB footnote), the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a site of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31) and a symbol of God’s judgment. Verse 48 quotes the last verse of Isaiah (66:24).
9.mean: Anyone who causes ‘one of these little ones who believe in Me’ to stumble would be better off thrown into the sea with a millstone round his neck. Then, in deliberately shocking pictures: if your hand, foot or eye causes you to sin, cut it off or pluck it out. ‘It is better for you to enter life crippled than to have two hands and go into hell, into the unquenchable fire’, ‘where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’’
9.big: Sin is so deadly that nothing is too precious to give up in order to avoid it; Jesus means the urgency, not literal self-harm.
9.diff: The nature of hell. The historic teaching of the Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches is that hell is eternal, conscious punishment: the Catholic Catechism ‘affirms the existence of hell and its eternity’, its chief punishment being ‘eternal separation from God’ (1035); the Westminster Confession speaks of ‘eternal torments’ (33.2). Another view, annihilationism or conditional immortality, holds that the unrepentant are finally destroyed, so that the fire is unquenchable in its effect rather than in endless suffering. It is held by Seventh-day Adventists and some evangelicals; John Stott made what one reviewer called ‘a well-argued, yet tentative, case’ for it in 1988. Both views take Jesus’ warnings with the utmost seriousness.

9.ctx: Salt preserved food and was added to every sacrifice (Leviticus 2:13). Salt from the Dead Sea area, mixed with other minerals, could lose its taste.
9.mean: ‘For everyone will be salted with fire.’ This is one of the hardest sayings in Mark. Most take it to mean that every disciple will be tested and purified by suffering, as sacrifices were salted. ‘Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.’ The disciples who argued about greatness (9:34) need the distinctive quality that makes them useful, and peace with each other.
9.big: Disciples will be refined by trial; they must keep their distinctive savour and live at peace.

10.ctx: Deuteronomy 24:1–4 regulated divorce. Rabbis debated its grounds: the school of Shammai allowed divorce only for serious sexual misconduct; the school of Hillel for almost any reason. Herod Antipas, in whose territory Jesus now was, had divorced to remarry (6:17–18).
10.mean: Pharisees ask, to test him, ‘Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife?’ Jesus asks what Moses commanded. ‘Moses permitted a man to write his wife a certificate of divorce and send her away.’ Jesus says Moses wrote that ‘because of your hardness of heart’. He goes back further, to creation: ‘God made them male and female’, and ‘the two will become one flesh.’ ‘Therefore what God has joined together, let man not separate.’ In private he tells the disciples: ‘Whoever divorces his wife and marries another woman commits adultery against her. And if a woman divorces her husband and marries another man, she commits adultery.’
10.big: Marriage is God’s work, joining a man and a woman as one for life; divorce is a concession to sin, not God’s design.
10.diff: Matthew’s account adds an exception, ‘except for sexual immorality’ (Matthew 19:9). Catholic teaching holds that ‘a ratified and consummated marriage cannot be dissolved by any human power or for any reason other than death’ (Catechism 2382); remarriage after civil divorce is not recognised while the first spouse lives (1650), though a marriage may be declared null if it was never valid. The Reformed confessions allow divorce and remarriage for ‘nothing but adultery, or such willful desertion as can no way be remedied’ (Westminster Confession 24.6, drawing on Matthew 19:9 and 1 Corinthians 7:15). The Orthodox Church, by ‘economy’ (pastoral concession), may permit a second marriage after divorce, with penitential prayers in the service. Many evangelicals hold one of these two Protestant positions; others are stricter. Wesley noted that Jesus’ words also condemn polygamy.

10.ctx: Parents brought children to rabbis to be blessed. The disciples thought Jesus had more important work.
10.mean: People bring little children for Jesus to touch, and the disciples rebuke them. Jesus is ‘indignant’, the only time Mark uses that word of him: ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these. Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.’ ‘And He took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them.’
10.big: The kingdom is received, not earned, by the dependent and the small, and Jesus has time for children.
10.diff: Children and baptism. Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Anglican, Methodist and Reformed churches baptise infants, and have often appealed to this passage. Calvin called it ‘a shield against the Anabaptists’: since baptism is ‘the pledge and figure of the forgiveness of sins, and likewise of adoption by God, it ought not to be denied to infants’. Baptists and many other evangelicals reply that Jesus blessed the children but did not baptise them, and that baptism is for those who profess faith (1689 Baptist Confession 29.2). All agree that children are welcome to Jesus.

10.ctx: Wealth was widely taken as a sign of God’s blessing. The camel and the ‘eye of a needle’ are a deliberately absurd picture of the impossible.
10.mean: A man runs up, kneels and asks, ‘Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ ‘Why do you call Me good?’ Jesus replies. ‘No one is good except God alone.’ He lists commandments about how we treat others. The man has kept them all since his youth. ‘Jesus looked at him, loved him’, and said: ‘There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.’ He goes away sad, ‘because he had great wealth.’ Jesus tells the astonished disciples, ‘It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.’ ‘Who then can be saved?’ ‘With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.’ To Peter he promises that whatever is given up for him will be repaid ‘a hundredfold in the present age…along with persecutions—and in the age to come, eternal life.’
10.big: No one can earn eternal life; salvation is impossible for us and possible only for God, and anything we hold onto above Jesus must go.
10.diff: ‘Why do you call Me good?’ Jesus is not denying that he is good or divine. Many have read it as an invitation to think through what calling him good implies. Calvin read it more simply: ‘Thou falsely callest me a good Master, unless thou acknowledgest that I have come from God.’ Sell everything. Most traditions read this as a specific call to a man whose wealth was his idol, not a rule for every believer. Catholic and Orthodox monasticism has seen in it a call to voluntary poverty for some (the ‘evangelical counsels’). All agree that Jesus must come first.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 10:17–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion
10.ctx: Jerusalem is ‘up’ from the Jordan valley: about 1,000 m of climb from Jericho.
10.mean: On the road up to Jerusalem Jesus walks ahead; the disciples are amazed and the followers afraid. For the third time he tells the Twelve what will happen, in the most detail yet: he will be handed to the chief priests and scribes, condemned to death, handed to the Gentiles, who ‘will mock Him and spit on Him and flog Him and kill Him. And after three days He will rise again.’
10.big: Jesus walked towards his death with open eyes and set purpose.

10.h: The Request of James and John
10.ctx: At the right and left hand of a king sat his most powerful ministers. In the Old Testament, the ‘cup’ is often the cup of God’s wrath (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15).
10.mean: Right after the passion prediction, James and John ask for the top seats ‘in Your glory.’ ‘You do not know what you are asking,’ Jesus replies. ‘Can you drink the cup I will drink, or be baptized with the baptism I will undergo?’ They say they can. He says they will share his sufferings (James was later executed, Acts 12:2), but the places of honour are not his to give. The other ten are indignant. Jesus contrasts Gentile rulers who ‘lord it over them’ with his way: ‘whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant’. ‘For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many.’
10.big: Jesus turns greatness upside down, and gives the key to his death: a ransom paid in his life, in place of many.
10.diff: A ransom ‘for many’. A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive; the Greek preposition means ‘in place of’. All traditions read verse 45 as a statement of Christ’s substitutionary, redeeming death; Calvin: ‘his life is the price of our redemption’. They differ over ‘many’. Reformed theology (‘definite’ or ‘particular’ redemption) holds that Christ’s death, sufficient for all, was intended to redeem effectually those the Father gave him (Canons of Dort II.3, 8). Arminian (Wesleyan) theology reads it as everyone: Wesley wrote, ‘Even for as many souls as needed such a ransom’. Catholic teaching likewise says ‘this last term is not restrictive’, and that Christ ‘died for all men without exception’ (Catechism 605).

10.ctx: Jericho lay on the pilgrim route from Galilee to Jerusalem via the Jordan valley, about 25 km from Jerusalem. Pilgrims for Passover would pass through in crowds.
10.mean: Leaving Jericho, Jesus passes a blind beggar, Bartimaeus, who shouts, ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!’, a messianic title, the first time anyone uses it in Mark. People tell him to be quiet; he shouts louder. Jesus stops: ‘Call him.’ Throwing off his cloak, perhaps all he owned, he jumps up. ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’, the same question Jesus asked James and John (10:36), who asked for glory. Bartimaeus asks, ‘let me see again.’ ‘Go,’ said Jesus, ‘your faith has healed you.’ ‘And immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road’, the road to Jerusalem and the cross.
10.big: A blind beggar sees who Jesus is more clearly than the disciples, and becomes a model of discipleship: he asks for mercy and follows.
10.diff: One blind man or two, leaving or entering? Matthew mentions two blind men (20:30); Luke says it happened as Jesus approached Jericho (18:35). Calvin rejected the idea of separate healings, called the difference a ‘puzzling contradiction’, and suggested the man called out as Jesus approached but was only heard as he left. Another suggestion is that there were two Jerichos, the old site and Herod’s new town a short distance away, so Jesus could be leaving one and approaching the other. Mark may name Bartimaeus because his readers knew him. Such differences in detail are normal in independent accounts.

b: Old Testament Jericho is the mound of Tell es-Sultan, beside a great spring, one of the oldest towns in the world. In New Testament times the main settlement lay about 2 km to the south, at Tulul Abu el-’Alayiq, where the Hasmonean kings and then Herod the Great built winter palaces with pools and gardens. Ehud Netzer excavated them between 1973 and 1987. This was the wealthy town where Zacchaeus collected taxes (Luke 19:1–10).

11.ctx: It is the Sunday before Passover, when Jerusalem’s population swelled with pilgrims. Zechariah 9:9 had promised Zion’s king would come ‘humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt’. Psalm 118, sung at the festivals, gave the crowd its words.
11.mean: Near Bethphage and Bethany, Jesus sends two disciples for a colt ‘on which no one has ever sat’, with the words ‘The Lord needs it and will return it shortly.’ Everything happens as he said. He rides into Jerusalem on it, people spread cloaks and branches on the road, and the crowds shout ‘Hosanna!’ (‘Save, we pray’), ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!’ ‘Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!’ He enters the temple, looks around at everything, and, since it is late, goes back to Bethany.
11.big: Jesus deliberately enters his city as its promised king, but as a humble king of peace, not a conqueror on a warhorse.

11.ctx: Fig trees around Jerusalem put out leaves in spring along with small early figs, which people ate. Leaves with no fruit at all signalled a barren tree. In the prophets the fig tree often stands for Israel (Jeremiah 8:13; Hosea 9:10).
11.mean: Hungry, Jesus sees a fig tree in leaf and finds nothing but leaves, ‘since it was not the season for figs.’ He says, ‘May no one ever eat of your fruit again.’ Mark wraps this story around the temple scene that follows, like a sandwich: a showy tree with no fruit, a magnificent temple with no true prayer.
11.big: An acted parable: impressive religion without the fruit God looks for faces judgment.
11.diff: Readers ask why Jesus cursed a tree for having no fruit out of season. Most interpreters, including Calvin, insist this was not temper: ‘it was not the fury of passion that led him to curse the tree’. It was a deliberate prophetic sign, like Jeremiah’s acted parables, of what was about to happen to the temple. The only miracle of judgment in the Gospels falls on a tree, not on people.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 11:11–24 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

11.ctx: The outer ‘Court of the Gentiles’ was the only part of the temple where non-Jews could pray. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice and had to pay the temple tax in Tyrian silver coins, so merchants and money changers set up there. John’s Gospel records a temple incident at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22).
11.mean: Jesus drives out the buyers and sellers, overturns the money changers’ tables and the dove-sellers’ seats, and stops people carrying goods through. He quotes Isaiah 56:7, ‘My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations’, and Jeremiah 7:11: ‘But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’’ Jeremiah had said that just before God destroyed the first temple. The chief priests and scribes start looking for a way to kill him, afraid because the crowd is amazed by his teaching.
11.big: Jesus acts with authority over God’s house and pronounces judgment on worship that shut out the nations and had become a hideout for corruption.
11.diff: Did Jesus clear the temple twice, at the beginning (John 2) and the end (Mark 11) of his ministry? Many conservative scholars think so, since the details differ. Many others think John placed one event early for theological reasons. The meaning is the same either way.

11.ctx: ‘This mountain’ is presumably the Mount of Olives or the temple mount itself, where they were walking.
11.mean: Next morning they see the fig tree ‘withered from its roots.’ Peter points it out. Jesus says, ‘Have faith in God.’ Whoever tells ‘this mountain’ to be thrown into the sea, without doubting, will see it happen. ‘Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours.’ And when you pray, forgive anyone you have something against, ‘so that your Father in heaven will forgive your trespasses as well.’
11.big: With the old temple facing judgment, Jesus points his followers to direct, confident prayer to God, and to forgiveness.
11.diff: ‘Believe that you have received it’. Some teachers (the ‘word of faith’ or prosperity movement) take this as a guarantee that anything asked with enough faith will be given. Most Christians of every tradition read it within the rest of Scripture: faith is in God, not in faith itself, and prayer is shaped by ‘not what I will, but what You will’ (14:36) and by asking according to his will (1 John 5:14).

11.ctx: The chief priests, scribes and elders made up the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. They controlled the temple Jesus had just disrupted.
11.mean: The leaders ask, ‘By what authority are You doing these things?’ Jesus asks in return: ‘John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from men?’ They are trapped. If they say heaven, why did they not believe John? If they say men, the people, who regarded John as a prophet, will turn on them. So they say, ‘We do not know.’ ‘Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.’
11.big: Those who would not respond honestly to God’s earlier messenger were in no position to judge Jesus’ authority.

12.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
12.ctx: Absentee landlords leasing vineyards to tenant farmers were common in Galilee. The opening echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7), where the vineyard is Israel.
12.mean: A man plants a vineyard and rents it out. At harvest he sends servants for his share; the tenants beat some and kill others. ‘Finally, having one beloved son, he sent him to them.’ They kill him too, reasoning, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours.’ The owner will destroy those tenants and give the vineyard to others. Jesus quotes Psalm 118: ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.’ The leaders know the parable is about them and want to arrest him, but fear the crowd.
12.big: Jesus presents himself as God’s beloved Son, the last and greatest messenger, whose rejection will become God’s way of building something new.

12.ctx: The tax in question was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, bitterly resented. A denarius bore the emperor Tiberius’s head and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus. To say ‘pay’ would anger nationalists; to say ‘don’t’ would be treason.
12.mean: Pharisees and Herodians flatter Jesus and then spring the trap: ‘Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar or not?’ He asks for a denarius: ‘Whose image is this? And whose inscription?’ ‘Caesar’s.’ ‘Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.’ The coin bears Caesar’s image, so give it back to him; human beings bear God’s image (Genesis 1:27), so give yourselves to God.
12.big: Governments have a real but limited claim; God’s claim is total.
12.diff: Christians agree that we owe governments taxes and lawful obedience (Romans 13:1–7), and that when rulers command what God forbids, ‘We must obey God rather than men’ (Acts 5:29). Calvin: if princes ‘claim any part of the authority of God, we ought not to obey them any farther than can be done without offending God’. Traditions differ on how far Christians should take part in government, politics, war and law: the Anabaptist tradition (Mennonites, Amish) has historically kept a separation from state power, while Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican and Catholic traditions see public office as a legitimate Christian calling (Westminster Confession 23).

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 12:13–17 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)

12.ctx: The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy. They accepted the five books of Moses as authoritative and denied the resurrection and angels (Acts 23:8). The law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5) required a man to marry his brother’s childless widow.
12.mean: The Sadducees pose a riddle: seven brothers each marry the same widow and die childless. ‘In the resurrection, then, whose wife will she be?’ Jesus replies that they know neither ‘the Scriptures or the power of God’. In the resurrection people ‘will neither marry nor be given in marriage. Instead, they will be like the angels in heaven.’ And from Moses himself, whom they accept: God told him at the burning bush, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’, long after those men had died. ‘He is not the God of the dead, but of the living. You are badly mistaken!’
12.big: God’s covenant faithfulness to his people does not end at death; resurrection life is not just this life continued, but transformed.

12.ctx: Rabbis counted 613 commandments in the Law and debated which were ‘weightier’. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–5) was recited by devout Jews twice daily.
12.mean: A scribe, impressed, asks, ‘Which commandment is the most important of all?’ Jesus answers with the Shema: ‘Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength.’ ‘The second is this: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’’ (Leviticus 19:18). The scribe agrees warmly: this is ‘more important than all burnt offerings and sacrifices.’ Jesus tells him, ‘You are not far from the kingdom of God.’
12.big: The whole Law comes down to wholehearted love for the one God and love for our neighbour.

12.ctx: Psalm 110 was understood as a psalm of David about the Messiah. It is the Old Testament passage most quoted in the New.
12.mean: Now Jesus asks the question. The scribes say the Christ is the son of David, which is true. But David, ‘Speaking by the Holy Spirit’, wrote, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I put Your enemies under Your feet.”’ ‘David himself calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?’ A son was never his father’s lord. The Messiah must be more than a human descendant of David.
12.big: The Christ is David’s son and David’s Lord: both human and divine.
12.diff: Some modern scholars argue that Psalm 110 was not written by David. Jesus’ argument assumes Davidic authorship, as the psalm’s heading states and as his hearers all accepted; it is also accepted by most conservative scholars.

12.ctx: Scribes were not paid for teaching; some depended on gifts from supporters, and some may have acted as legal trustees for widows’ estates.
12.mean: ‘Watch out for the scribes.’ They love long robes, greetings in the market, the best seats in synagogues and at banquets. ‘They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.’
12.big: Religious status used for self-display and gain, especially at the expense of the vulnerable, brings the heaviest judgment.

12.ctx: Collection chests for offerings stood in the temple courts. The ‘two small copper coins’ were lepta, the smallest coins in circulation (BSB footnote).
12.mean: Jesus watches the crowd giving. The rich put in large sums. A poor widow puts in two tiny coins. ‘Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put more than all the others into the treasury. For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.’
12.big: God measures giving not by the amount but by what it costs and the heart behind it.
12.diff: This is usually read as praise of the widow’s total devotion. Some commentators also see a lament, following straight on from 12:40: a system that took a poor widow’s last coins was devouring widows’ houses. Both readings can stand together.

13.ctx: Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world, faced with white stone and gold. Some of its foundation stones, still visible in the Western Wall, weigh many tons.
13.mean: A disciple marvels at the temple’s stones and buildings. Jesus says, ‘Not one stone here will be left on another; every one will be thrown down.’ On the Mount of Olives, facing the temple, four disciples ask privately, ‘when will these things happen? And what will be the sign’? Jesus’ first concern is that they are not deceived: many will come in his name. Wars, earthquakes and famines will come, but ‘the end is still to come. …These are the beginning of birth pains.’
13.big: Jesus foretells the temple’s destruction and warns his followers not to be misled into thinking every disaster means the end.

b: In AD 66 the Jews revolted against Rome. In AD 70 the Roman general Titus besieged Jerusalem. Josephus, who was with the Roman army, describes how on the tenth day of the month Ab the temple was set on fire by a Roman soldier, against Titus’s wishes, and burned. The city was largely destroyed. Herod’s great temple, completed only in the early 60s, stood for just a few years in its finished form.

Parts of Herod’s massive retaining walls still stand, most famously the Western Wall, in places about 20 m high. The temple building itself, which stood on the platform above, was destroyed and has never been rebuilt.
Eusebius records that before the war the Jerusalem church, warned by a revelation, left the city for Pella, east of the Jordan, which fits Jesus’ warning to ‘flee to the mountains’ (13:14).

13.ctx: Mark’s first readers lived through what Jesus describes here; Christians in Rome were betrayed and killed under Nero.
13.mean: ‘So be on your guard.’ They will be handed over to councils, beaten in synagogues, brought before governors and kings ‘as witnesses to them.’ ‘And the gospel must first be proclaimed to all the nations.’ When arrested, they need not prepare speeches: ‘it will not be you speaking, but the Holy Spirit.’ Families will betray each other. ‘You will be hated by everyone because of My name, but the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.’
13.big: Persecution will not stop the gospel; it becomes an occasion for testimony, and the Spirit helps those who stand firm.

13.ctx: The phrase comes from Daniel (9:27; 11:31; 12:11). In 167 BC the Greek king Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the temple (1 Maccabees 1:54), which Jews saw as its fulfilment.
13.mean: ‘So when you see the abomination of desolation standing where it should not be (let the reader understand), then let those who are in Judea flee to the mountains.’ Do not stop to collect anything. ‘How miserable those days will be for pregnant and nursing mothers!’ ‘Pray that this will not occur in the winter.’ It will be a time of unequalled distress, but God has cut the days short ‘for the sake of the elect’. False Christs and false prophets will do signs to deceive ‘even the elect, if that were possible.’ ‘So be on your guard; I have told you everything in advance.’
13.big: When the sacrilege comes, run: Jesus gives his followers practical warning so that they can escape and not be deceived.
13.diff: What is the ‘abomination’, and when? Christians read this chapter in several ways. Many see verses 5–23 as fulfilled in the Jewish War and the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, with the abomination being the Roman armies, the Zealots’ desecration of the temple, or Titus’s troops in it; Calvin understood the abomination as the pollution of the temple that brought its destruction. Others see a double reference, to AD 70 and to the end times. Dispensational premillennialists (for example Dallas Theological Seminary) expect a future tribulation in which the Antichrist will desecrate a rebuilt temple. Many scholars think Mark’s version focuses on AD 70, while Matthew’s (which asks about ‘the end of the age’, Matthew 24:3) points to both.

13.h: The Return of the Son of Man
13.ctx: The language of darkened sun and falling stars comes from the prophets (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4; Joel 2:10), where it described God’s judgment on nations. Daniel 7:13 pictures ‘one like a son of man’ coming with the clouds of heaven.
13.mean: ‘But in those days, after that tribulation’, the sun and moon will be darkened, the stars will fall, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. ‘At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds with great power and glory. And He will send out the angels to gather His elect from the four winds’.
13.big: History does not end in chaos: the Son of Man will come in glory and gather all his people.
13.diff: Second coming or AD 70? Most Christians, with Calvin, read these verses as Christ’s personal return at the end of history; Calvin said the ‘tribulation’ is not just the fall of Jerusalem but ‘a general recapitulation of all the evils’ Christ had spoken of. Some scholars argue that, as in the prophets, the cosmic language describes the fall of Jerusalem, and that the Son of Man ‘coming’ is his vindication and enthronement (as in Daniel 7, where he comes to God). All Christian traditions confess that Christ ‘shall come again with glory to judge the quick and the dead’ (Nicene Creed).

13.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree
13.ctx: Most trees in Palestine are evergreen; the fig loses its leaves in winter, so new leaves were a sure sign of approaching summer.
13.mean: When the fig tree’s branches sprout leaves, you know summer is near. ‘So also, when you see these things happening, know that He is near, right at the door. Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.’
13.big: Jesus’ words are more permanent than the universe.
13.diff: ‘This generation’. Calvin took it to mean the people then living, who would see the destruction of the temple: ‘within fifty years the city was destroyed and the temple was razed’. Wesley agreed that ‘all these things’ relate to ‘the temple and the city’. Others take ‘generation’ to mean the Jewish people or the generation alive when the final signs begin. The first view is the most natural reading of the word and allows Jesus to be entirely accurate.

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Mark 13

13.ctx: A doorkeeper had to be ready to open the door whenever the master arrived, day or night. The four times named are the four Roman night watches.
13.mean: ‘No one knows about that day or hour, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father.’ So: ‘Be on your guard and stay alert!’ Like servants left in charge while the master is away, ‘keep watch, because you do not know when the master of the house will return’. ‘And what I say to you, I say to everyone: Keep watch!’
13.big: The right response to Christ’s return is not calculating dates but faithful readiness.
13.diff: How could the Son not know? This verse was used by Arians in the 4th century to deny Christ’s full deity. The church answered that Christ is one person with two natures, divine and human (Chalcedon, 451), and that he speaks here according to his human nature, in which he truly grew in knowledge (Luke 2:52). Calvin: Christ, ‘who knew all things’, ‘was ignorant of something in respect of his perception as a man’. Wesley: ‘Not as man: as man he was no more omniscient than omnipresent. But as God he knows all the circumstances of it.’ Every attempt to set a date for the return has been wrong.

14.ctx: Passover commemorated Israel’s rescue from Egypt; the Feast of Unleavened Bread followed for seven days. Josephus says the huge festival crowds made the Roman authorities nervous.
14.mean: Two days before Passover, the chief priests and scribes look for ‘a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him. “But not during the feast,” they said, “or there may be a riot among the people.”’
14.big: The authorities planned to avoid the feast; God’s plan placed Jesus’ death at Passover.

14.ctx: Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. Three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages for a labourer. John’s Gospel names the woman as Mary of Bethany (John 12:1–8).
14.mean: At dinner in Bethany at the home of Simon the Leper, a woman breaks open an alabaster jar of pure nard and pours it on Jesus’ head. Some are indignant at the waste: it could have been sold for the poor. Jesus defends her: ‘She has done a beautiful deed to Me. The poor you will always have with you’ (echoing Deuteronomy 15:11, which commands generosity to them), ‘But you will not always have Me. She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.’ And wherever the gospel is preached, her act will be told in her memory.
14.big: Extravagant love for Jesus is never wasted; she alone seems to have understood that he was going to die.

14.ctx: ‘Iscariot’ may mean ‘man from Kerioth’, a town in Judea. Mark sets Judas’s act right beside the woman’s devotion.
14.mean: ‘Then Judas Iscariot, one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests to betray Jesus to them.’ They are delighted and promise him money, and he looks for an opportunity.
14.big: The contrast is stark: one gives costly love, another sells his master.

14.ctx: The Passover lambs were sacrificed in the temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan and eaten that evening inside the city walls. A man carrying a water jar would stand out, as this was usually women’s work.
14.mean: On the day the Passover lamb was sacrificed, the disciples ask where to prepare the meal. Jesus sends two of them: a man carrying a jug of water will meet them; they are to follow him and ask the owner of the house for the guest room. ‘And he will show you a large upper room, furnished and ready.’ It happens just as he said.
14.big: Jesus is in control of the events leading to his death; he is not a victim of circumstances.
14.diff: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal? Mark, Matthew and Luke clearly present it as one. John’s Gospel seems to place Jesus’ death on the day the lambs were killed, before the Passover meal (John 18:28; 19:14). Scholars such as Joachim Jeremias have defended the Synoptic dating; others think John’s timing is historical. Several harmonisations have been proposed, for example that John’s references are to the festival week as a whole, or that different groups followed different calendars. Either way, all four Gospels connect Jesus’ death with Passover (compare 1 Corinthians 5:7).

src.l: ‘Last Supper’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Jeremias)

14.ctx: At Passover the head of the household explained the meaning of the bread and the cups of wine in terms of the exodus. Jesus reinterprets them in terms of himself.
14.mean: As they eat, Jesus says one of them will betray him; they ask, one by one, ‘Surely not I?’ ‘The Son of Man will go just as it is written about Him, but woe to that man by whom He is betrayed!’ Then: ‘Jesus took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, “Take it; this is My body.”’ He takes the cup, gives thanks, and they all drink: ‘This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.’ (Compare Exodus 24:8, where Moses sealed the covenant with blood.) He will not drink wine again ‘until that day when I drink it anew in the kingdom of God.’ They sing a hymn (probably Psalms 115–118) and go out to the Mount of Olives.
14.big: Jesus gives his followers a meal that interprets his death: his body given and his blood poured out to make a new covenant for many.
14.diff: ‘This is My body’. All Christians keep this meal; they differ on how Christ is present. Catholic teaching holds that the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood (transubstantiation), so that he is ‘truly, really, and substantially contained’ (Catechism 1374). Orthodox teaching affirms a real change but does not define how. Lutherans confess ‘the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the bread and wine’. Reformed theology holds that Christ is truly received spiritually by faith; Calvin: ‘we must not suppose that there is any change of the substance’, since sacramental language names the sign by the thing signified. Many Baptist and other evangelical churches stress remembrance. See the glossary entry.

14.ctx: Zechariah 13:7 speaks of the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered.
14.mean: ‘You will all fall away’, Jesus says, quoting Zechariah: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’ ‘But after I have risen, I will go ahead of you into Galilee.’ Peter insists, ‘Even if all fall away, I never will.’ Jesus tells him that before the rooster crows twice that night he will deny him three times. Peter protests that he would die first, and all the others say the same.
14.big: Jesus knew his friends would fail him, and promised to meet them again before they had even failed.

14.ctx: Gethsemane means ‘oil press’. It was a garden or olive grove on the lower slopes of the Mount of Olives, across the Kidron Valley from the temple. The exact spot is not known. In the Old Testament ‘the cup’ is often the cup of God’s wrath (Isaiah 51:17).
14.mean: Jesus takes Peter, James and John further in, and ‘began to be deeply troubled and distressed.’ ‘My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death’, he tells them. He falls to the ground and prays: ‘Abba, Father,’ ‘all things are possible for You. Take this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.’ ‘Abba’ is the Aramaic word a child used for a father. Three times he returns and finds them asleep. ‘Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak.’ Finally: ‘The hour has come…Rise, let us go. See, My betrayer is approaching!’
14.big: Jesus truly dreaded the cross, and chose it in obedience to his Father; his friends slept through his agony.
14.diff: Two wills? Jesus’ prayer shows a real human will that shrank from suffering and submitted to the Father. Against those who said Christ had only one (divine) will, the Third Council of Constantinople (681), accepted by Orthodox, Catholics and most Protestants, confessed ‘two natural wills’ in Christ, divine and human, not ‘contrary or opposed one to the other’. Calvin: Christ ‘restrains his feelings at the very outset, and quickly brings himself into a state of obedience’.

b: The Gospels do not give an exact location, and the landscape has changed since the Romans cut down the trees round Jerusalem during the siege of AD 70. At least four sites are shown today on the western slope of the Mount of Olives. The traditional one, kept by the Franciscans, has the Church of All Nations and a garden of very old olive trees. It is reasonably close to where the Gospels place the garden, but cannot be confirmed.

14.ctx: A kiss was the normal greeting of a disciple to his teacher. The arresting party came from the chief priests, not Rome.
14.mean: Judas arrives with an armed crowd sent by the chief priests, scribes and elders. His signal: ‘The One I kiss is the man’. ‘Rabbi!’ he says, and kisses him. One bystander draws a sword and cuts off the ear of the high priest’s servant (John names him Peter). Jesus asks why they come with swords and clubs as if he were an outlaw, when he taught openly in the temple every day: ‘But this has happened that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.’ ‘Then everyone deserted Him and fled.’ A young man in only a linen cloth is grabbed, and runs off naked.
14.big: Betrayed with a kiss and abandoned by all, Jesus goes to his death alone, as Scripture said.
14.diff: The young man (verses 51–52) appears only in Mark. A long-standing suggestion is that it was Mark himself, adding a quiet signature to his own Gospel; some link this with the house of Mark’s mother in Jerusalem (Acts 12:12). It cannot be proved. Calvin thought he was a neighbour roused by the noise who came out to help.

14.ctx: The Sanhedrin was the Jewish supreme council of seventy-one members, chaired by the high priest. Under Roman rule it could not carry out a death sentence on its own authority (John 18:31).
14.mean: Jesus is taken to the high priest. Peter follows at a distance into the courtyard. The council looks for testimony to justify death, but the witnesses contradict each other, even about his saying on destroying the temple. The high priest demands an answer; Jesus is silent. Then: ‘Are You the Christ, the Son of the Blessed One?’ ‘I am,’ said Jesus, ‘and you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.’ He combines Psalm 110:1 and Daniel 7:13, claiming to share God’s throne and to be the coming judge. The high priest tears his clothes: ‘You have heard the blasphemy.’ They condemn him, spit on him, blindfold and beat him, and taunt, ‘Prophesy!’, while just outside, his prophecy about Peter is coming true.
14.big: At his trial Jesus openly claims to be the Messiah, the Son of God and the Son of Man who will share God’s throne; that claim is why he was condemned.

b: Mark does not name the high priest, but Matthew and John do: Caiaphas. Josephus calls him ‘Joseph Caiaphas’ and records his appointment under the governor Valerius Gratus. He held office from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long time, covering the whole of Pilate’s governorship.

The Caiaphas ossuary (Widely accepted). In 1990 builders accidentally uncovered a family tomb in modern Jerusalem. One finely decorated bone box (ossuary) is inscribed ‘Joseph, son of Caiaphas’. Many scholars think it is the high priest’s. It cannot be certain, because Joseph was a common name and the inscription does not mention the high priesthood.

b: The Mishnah, a collection of Jewish law written down about AD 200, lays down rules for capital trials: they are to be held in the daytime, a guilty verdict cannot be given on the same day as the trial, and so such trials are not held on the eve of a Sabbath or festival. Mark’s account, a night hearing at the high priest’s house followed by an early-morning decision (15:1), breaks several of these rules.

Scholars disagree on what this means. Some think the Mishnah’s rules reflect later, idealised practice and may not have applied in Jesus’ day, when the Sadducean high priests controlled the court. Others think the night hearing was an informal inquiry to prepare charges for Pilate rather than a formal trial. Others again see a deliberately rushed and irregular proceeding by leaders determined to act before the festival. Mark himself presents it as unjust, with false witnesses and a predetermined result.

14.ctx: Galileans had a distinctive accent (compare Matthew 26:73). Mark’s account, traditionally drawn from Peter’s own preaching, spares him nothing.
14.mean: Below in the courtyard a servant girl says to Peter, ‘You also were with Jesus the Nazarene.’ He denies it. She says it again to the bystanders; he denies it again. Then the bystanders: ‘Surely you are one of them, for you too are a Galilean.’ ‘But he began to curse and swear, “I do not know this man of whom you speak!”’ The rooster crows a second time. Peter remembers Jesus’ words, ‘And he broke down and wept.’
14.big: The leader of the apostles failed completely; his story, told openly, gives hope to every failed disciple (compare 16:7).

15.ctx: Roman officials began work at dawn. Pilate normally lived at Caesarea and came up to Jerusalem at festivals to keep order. The Sanhedrin needed a political charge: claiming to be ‘King of the Jews’ was rebellion against Caesar.
15.mean: At dawn the whole Sanhedrin binds Jesus and hands him over to Pilate. ‘Are You the King of the Jews?’ ‘You have said so’, Jesus replies, an answer that accepts the title but on his own terms. The chief priests accuse him of many things; Jesus makes no further reply, ‘to Pilate’s amazement.’
15.big: Jesus’ silence before his accusers recalls the servant of Isaiah 53:7, who ‘did not open His mouth’.

b: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36/37 and is one of the best-attested figures of the period. Josephus describes him bringing Roman standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem by night, backing down when crowds offered to die rather than see their law broken, and later using temple funds for an aqueduct and having protesters clubbed. The Roman historian Tacitus writes that ‘Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus’.

The Pilate Stone. In 1961 Italian archaeologists excavating the theatre at Caesarea Maritima found a reused limestone block with a Latin inscription recording that Pilate dedicated a building in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It gives his title as ‘prefect of Judea’ and is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

15.ctx: Barabbas (‘son of the father’) had been arrested with rebels who had committed murder in an uprising.
15.mean: Pilate’s custom was to release a prisoner of the people’s choosing at the feast. A crowd comes asking him to keep the custom. Pilate offers ‘the King of the Jews’, knowing ‘it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.’ But the chief priests stir up the crowd to ask for Barabbas instead.
15.big: The guilty man goes free and the innocent one takes his place: a picture of what Jesus’ death means.

b: No ancient source outside the Gospels mentions a custom of releasing a prisoner at Passover, and Roman governors were not known for such concessions; so some scholars doubt it. Others point out that Roman officials did sometimes grant amnesties, that the custom may have been local and short-lived, and that the Mishnah, discussing who may share in the Passover lamb, includes ‘one whom the governing body promised to release from prison on the night of Passover’, which suggests such releases did happen. All four Gospels record the Barabbas episode.

15.ctx: Roman flogging, with a whip of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, often preceded crucifixion. Some victims died under it.
15.mean: ‘What then do you want me to do with the One you call the King of the Jews?’ ‘Crucify Him!’ ‘Why?’ asked Pilate. ‘What evil has He done?’ They shout louder. ‘And wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them. But he had Jesus flogged, and handed Him over to be crucified.’
15.big: Pilate knew Jesus was innocent and condemned him anyway, to keep the crowd quiet.

15.ctx: The ‘company’ (Latin cohort) could number several hundred soldiers. Purple was the colour of royalty.
15.mean: The soldiers take Jesus into the Praetorium and call the whole company together. They dress him in purple, twist a crown of thorns onto his head and salute him: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ They beat his head with a staff, spit on him and kneel in mock homage, then put his own clothes back on him and lead him out to crucify him.
15.big: The soldiers mock Jesus as king, and without knowing it tell the truth.

b: Christian tradition since the Middle Ages placed the trial at the Antonia Fortress beside the temple, and visitors are still shown a paved area under the Sisters of Zion convent there. Archaeologists now date that pavement to the 2nd century AD, after Jesus’ time.

Most scholars now think Pilate stayed at Herod’s former palace on the western hill when he came to Jerusalem, and that this is the ‘Praetorium’ (Mark 15:16). Josephus says a later governor, Florus, set up his judgment seat there. The exact spot is not certain.

15.ctx: Cyrene was in North Africa (modern Libya), with a large Jewish community. Condemned men carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. Wine mixed with myrrh may have been a drink to dull pain.
15.mean: The soldiers force a passer-by, Simon of Cyrene, ‘the father of Alexander and Rufus’, to carry the cross. At Golgotha (‘The Place of the Skull’) they offer Jesus drugged wine; he refuses it. ‘And they crucified Him.’ Mark gives the bare fact, no details of the agony. They gamble for his clothes (compare Psalm 22:18). It is ‘the third hour’, about 9 a.m. The charge reads: ‘THE KING OF THE JEWS.’ Two robbers are crucified on either side. Passers-by, chief priests and even the other crucified men mock him: ‘He saved others, but He cannot save Himself!’ They speak more truly than they know: he will not save himself, in order to save others.
15.big: The King is enthroned on a cross between two criminals, mocked by everyone, refusing to save himself so that he can save others.
15.diff: ‘The third hour’. John says Jesus was still before Pilate ‘about the sixth hour’ (John 19:14). People then did not keep exact time, and some suggest Mark gives the start of the whole process at the third-hour mark, and John the approximate time of sentence by another reckoning. It is an acknowledged difficulty. Alexander and Rufus were evidently known to Mark’s readers; Rufus may be the one greeted in Romans 16:13.

b: Crucifixion was the Romans’ most shameful punishment, used for slaves and rebels. Ancient writers describe it often, but physical remains are rare, because bodies were usually left to decay or thrown away. In 1968, in a tomb at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in northern Jerusalem, archaeologists found an ossuary containing the bones of a crucified man from the 1st century AD, with an iron nail about 11.5 cm long still driven through his heel bone. It confirms that victims were nailed, and that a crucified Jew could be given a proper family burial, as Jesus was.

15.ctx: ‘The sixth hour until the ninth hour’ is noon to 3 p.m. Psalm 22, which begins with Jesus’ cry, moves from abandonment to praise and the nations turning to God. The temple veil separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place, which only the high priest could enter, once a year.
15.mean: Darkness covers the land for three hours. At three, Jesus cries out in Aramaic: ‘Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?’, ‘My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?’ Some think he is calling Elijah; one offers him sour wine on a sponge. ‘But Jesus let out a loud cry and breathed His last. And the veil of the temple was torn in two from top to bottom’: torn by God, from above. The centurion who saw how he died says, ‘Truly this man was the Son of God!’ Women who had followed him from Galilee watch from a distance: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Joses, Salome and many others.
15.big: Jesus bears God-forsakenness in our place; the way into God’s presence is opened; and a Gentile soldier makes the confession the whole Gospel has been building towards.
15.diff: ‘Why have You forsaken Me?’ Christians agree that Jesus was not mistaken or despairing of God, and that the Trinity was not split. Reformed and many Protestant theologians see here the experience of God’s judgment on sin as our substitute; Calvin: ‘having undertaken to be our surety, he resolved actually to undergo in our room the judgment of God’, yet ‘in his heart faith remained firm’. Others, including many Catholic and Orthodox writers, emphasise that Jesus prays the whole of Psalm 22, which ends in trust and triumph, and that he entered fully into human desolation. These are complementary rather than opposed.

b: Julius Africanus, a Christian chronographer writing about AD 220, says that a historian named Thallus, in the third book of his history, explained this darkness as an eclipse of the sun. Africanus objected that an eclipse is impossible at Passover, which falls at full moon. If Thallus wrote in the 1st century, as some think, this would show that the darkness at Jesus’ death was already being discussed by non-Christians. But Thallus’s work is lost, we know of it only through Africanus, and its date and exact wording are uncertain. A darkness of three hours cannot have been a solar eclipse; the Gospels present it as a sign from God.

15.ctx: Jewish law required the bodies of the executed to be buried before nightfall (Deuteronomy 21:23), and the Sabbath began at sunset on Friday. Romans often left crucified bodies on the cross as a warning.
15.mean: Joseph of Arimathea, ‘a prominent Council member who himself was waiting for the kingdom of God’, boldly asks Pilate for the body. Pilate is surprised that Jesus is already dead and checks with the centurion. Joseph buys a linen cloth, takes the body down, wraps it and lays it in a tomb cut out of the rock, and rolls a stone against the entrance. Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses watch where he is laid.
15.big: Jesus truly died and was truly buried, confirmed by a Roman officer and witnessed by the women who would find the tomb empty.

hist.t: Where are Golgotha and the tomb?
b: Two sites are shown today.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre. In the 4th century the emperor Constantine built a church over a site local Christians identified, under a temple Hadrian had built about AD 135. It is now inside the Old City walls, but excavations, including Kathleen Kenyon’s in the 1960s, showed that in Jesus’ time the area was an old quarry outside the walls, with rock-cut tombs of the 1st century. Most archaeologists regard it as the most likely location.

The Garden Tomb. North of the Damascus Gate, identified by General Charles Gordon in 1883, it is a peaceful place to visit. But excavations by Gabriel Barkay and Amos Kloner indicate that the tomb was first cut in the Iron Age (8th–7th centuries BC), so it would not have been a new tomb in Jesus’ day. Few archaeologists now think it was Jesus’ tomb.

16.ctx: Spices were brought to honour the dead and lessen the smell of decay; the women did not expect a resurrection. In that culture women were not normally accepted as legal witnesses; Josephus says their testimony should not be admitted.
16.mean: Early on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome go with spices, wondering who will roll away the stone. It has already been rolled away. Inside they see ‘a young man dressed in a white robe’. ‘Do not be alarmed. You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, who was crucified. He has risen! He is not here! See the place where they put Him.’ ‘But go, tell His disciples and Peter’, ‘and Peter’, who had denied him, ‘He is going ahead of you into Galilee.’ The women flee from the tomb, ‘trembling and bewildered. And in their fear they did not say a word to anyone.’
16.big: The crucified Jesus has risen; and the first message of the risen Lord includes a special word for the disciple who failed him.
16.diff: Why women? If the early Christians had invented the story, they would hardly have made women, whose testimony counted for little in that culture, the first witnesses of the empty tomb. An abrupt ending. The best manuscripts end the Gospel at verse 8 (see the note on verses 9–20). Mark had already told his readers that the disciples would see Jesus in Galilee (14:28; 16:7); the women’s silence was evidently temporary, since the message got out.

16.ctx: Verses 9–20 are the ‘longer ending’ of Mark. The BSB prints them with a note that some early manuscripts end at verse 8 (see the drop-down below).
16.mean: Jesus appears first to Mary Magdalene, ‘from whom He had driven out seven demons’ (compare Luke 8:2; John 20:11–18). She tells the mourning disciples, ‘they did not believe it.’
16.big: The first witness of the risen Jesus was a woman he had set free, and the disciples’ first response was unbelief.

b: The evidence. The two oldest complete manuscripts of Mark, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century), end at 16:8, and no manuscript up to the 4th century ends differently. From the 5th century the ‘longer ending’ (verses 9–20) appears and soon becomes standard in almost all later copies, which is why it is in the King James Version. A few manuscripts have a short ending instead (BSB footnote), or both. The longer ending’s vocabulary and style differ from the rest of Mark, and its contents read like a summary of appearances found in the other Gospels and Acts. For these reasons virtually all New Testament scholars regard it as an early addition rather than part of what Mark wrote. Modern Bibles, including the BSB, print it with a note.

The case for the longer ending (a minority view). The ending is very old. Irenaeus, about AD 180, quotes verse 19 and says it comes ‘towards the conclusion of his Gospel’, and it is in the great majority of all Greek manuscripts. Nicholas Lunn (2014) argues that it is original: that early writers knew it before our oldest manuscripts were copied, that its unusual words fall within the normal range for undisputed passages of Mark, that it contains characteristic Markan features, and that it was dropped in Egypt in the 2nd century. Craig Evans, who long held the opposite view, said Lunn’s book had ‘thoroughly shaken’ it. Calvin, like most of the church before the 19th century, commented on it as Mark’s.

Where that leaves us. Either Mark meant to end at verse 8, with frightened women and an empty tomb, leaving readers to answer for themselves; or his original ending was lost early, perhaps from the outer end of a damaged scroll or codex. Either way, nothing in verses 9–20 teaches anything not found elsewhere in Scripture, except the promise about snakes and poison, and no Christian doctrine depends on it. Christians who read it as Scripture and those who do not agree on the resurrection appearances, the commission and the ascension, all of which the other Gospels and Acts record.

16.ctx: Part of the longer ending; this summarises the Emmaus story told in full in Luke 24:13–35.
16.mean: ‘After this, Jesus appeared in a different form to two of them as they walked along in the country.’ They report it, ‘but they did not believe them either.’
16.big: The disciples did not invent the resurrection out of wishful thinking; they had to be convinced against their expectations.

16.ctx: Part of the longer ending. Compare Matthew 28:18–20; Luke 24:46–49; Acts 1:8.
16.mean: Jesus appears to the Eleven at a meal and rebukes their unbelief. ‘Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned.’ Signs will accompany believers: driving out demons, new tongues, picking up snakes, drinking poison unharmed, healing the sick.
16.big: The risen Jesus sends his unbelieving, rebuked disciples to the whole world with the good news.
16.diff: ‘Believes and is baptized’. Note that condemnation is linked to not believing, not to lack of baptism. Catholic teaching cites this to show that ‘Baptism is necessary for salvation’ for those who have heard the gospel (Catechism 1257). Lutherans cite it for baptism’s saving power received by faith (Small Catechism). Reformed and Baptist Christians hold that baptism is commanded but that salvation is not ‘so inseparably annexed unto it’ that no one can be saved without it (Westminster Confession 28.5). The signs. Calvin thought ‘it is more probable that miracles were promised only for a time, in order to give luster to the gospel, while it was new’. Pentecostals expect such signs today. Paul was bitten by a snake unharmed (Acts 28:3–6), but nothing here commands deliberately handling snakes or drinking poison, as a few fringe groups have done.
